bio.en: Ken Norton spent 14 years at Google leading product teams behind Google Docs, Calendar, and Maps, and now works full-time as an executive coach for product leaders.
bio.zh: 肯·诺顿（Ken Norton）在 Google 工作了 14 年，领导过 Google Docs、Calendar 和 Maps 等产品团队，如今是全职的产品高管教练。

summary.en: Ken emphasizes that product management is leadership from day one, even without formal authority. He discusses the creative versus reactive mindset and why the art of PM-ing matters more than the science. The episode covers overcoming imposter syndrome, common PM blind spots, and how to find and evaluate a good coach.
summary.zh: 肯强调，产品经理从第一天起就是领导者，即便没有正式职权。他探讨了"创造性"与"被动反应"两种心态，以及为何产品管理的"艺术"比"科学"更重要。本期涵盖如何克服冒名顶替综合征、PM 常见的盲点，以及如何找到并评估一位好教练。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Part of what I think is pretty exciting about product management is you are a leader from day one in product management. There's leadership all over the place, but that's your job. You're a leader. You don't have any formal authority, but you're a leader. You're expected to lead
turns.zh: 对我来说，产品管理最令人兴奋的一点在于，从你踏入这个领域的第一天起，你就是一名领导者。领导力无处不在，但这份职责就是你的使命。你就是领导者。虽然没有正式的职权，但你必须发挥领导作用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Over his 14-year career at Google. Ken Norton led product teams at built Google Docs, Google Calendar, Google Maps, and even did a stint at Google Ventures. The products that he's helped craft are now used by over three billion people. (00:00:37): Today Ken is a full-time executive coach specializing at working with product leaders. In our conversation, we cover the creative versus reactive mindset, why the art of product management is much more important than the science of product management, how to get over imposter syndrome, the most common PM blind spots, how to find a coach and how to know if a coach is right for you, and so much more. I hope that you enjoy this episode with Ken Norton. (00:01:05): If you're setting up your analytics stack but you're not using Amplitude, what are you doing? Amplitude is the number one most popular analytics solution in the world, used by both big companies like Shopify, Instacart, and Atlassian, and also most tech startups. Amplitude has everything you need, including a powerful and fully self-service analytics product, an experimentation platform, and even an integrated customer data platform to help you understand your users like never before. (00:01:33): Give your teams self-service product data to understand your users, drive conversions, and increase engagement, growth, and revenue. Get your vanity metrics, trust your data, work smarter, and grow your business. Try Amplitude for free. Just visit amplitude.com to get started. (00:01:53): Have you heard of Lenny's Job Board? Well, if you're hiring or open to a new gig, have I got the site for you, lennysjobs.com. If you're a hiring manager, sign up and get access to hundreds of hand-curated people who are open to new opportunities. Thousands of people apply. And I personally review and accept just 10% of them to be part of this collective. You won't find a better place to hire product managers and growth people. (00:02:18): If you're someone who's looking around for someone new, join the collective. It's free. You can be anonymous and hide yourself from any company. You can also leave anytime. You'll only hear from companies that you want to hear from. Check out lennysjobs.com to learn more. (00:02:38): Welcome to the podcast, Ken. I am so honored to have you here. You're such a legend of product managers and product management circles. Your writing has had so much influence on so many people, including myself. If nothing else, you've led to many donuts being purchased by tech companies over the years. So thanks for being here.
turns.zh: 在谷歌14年的职业生涯中，肯·诺顿领导的产品团队开发了Google Docs、Google Calendar、Google Maps等产品，还曾在Google Ventures任职。他参与打造的产品如今已被超过30亿人使用。（00:00:37）：如今，肯是一名专注于产品领导者的全职高管教练。在对话中，我们探讨了创造性思维与被动反应思维的对比，产品管理的艺术为何比科学更为重要，如何克服冒名顶替综合症，最常见的产品管理盲点，如何选择教练以及如何判断教练是否适合自己等诸多话题。希望您能喜欢与肯·诺顿的这期对话。（00:01:05）：如果您正在搭建分析框架却不使用Amplitude，那您在做什么？Amplitude是全球最受欢迎的分析解决方案，既被Shopify、Instacart、Atlassian等大型企业采用，也深受多数科技初创公司的青睐。Amplitude提供您所需的一切，包括强大且完全自助的分析产品、实验平台，甚至集成的客户数据平台，助您前所未有地了解用户。（00:01:33）：赋予团队自助获取产品数据的能力，以便深入理解用户、推动转化并提升用户参与度、增长和收益。获取虚荣指标、信任数据、更高效工作并发展业务。免费试用Amplitude，访问amplitude.com即可开始。（00:01:53）：您听说过Lenny's Job Board吗？如果您正在招聘或寻求新机会，我为您推荐lennysjobs.com。如果您是招聘经理，注册即可访问数百名渴望新机遇的精选人才。数千人申请该平台，而我亲自筛选并接纳其中10%的人才加入这个社区。您找不到比这更好的招聘产品经理和增长团队的平台了。（00:02:18）：欢迎来到播客，肯。很荣幸能邀请到您。您是产品经理和产品管理领域的传奇人物。您的作品对包括我在内的许多人产生了深远影响。即便不计其他，您这些年也让科技公司买了不少甜甜圈呢。所以感谢您的到来。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Thank you and thanks for having me. The feeling's mutual. Obviously a big fan of your work and all the things you've done for the community and this podcast, which has been fantastic. So humbled and excited to be here. Yes, I do think that I'm at least maybe partially responsible for at least a lot of consumption of donuts over these years.
turns.zh: 谢谢您，也感谢您的邀请。这种感觉是相互的。显然，我是您工作的忠实粉丝，您为社区和这个播客所做的一切都太棒了。能来这里既荣幸又兴奋。是的，我确实认为这些年我至少对人们消费甜甜圈的量负有部分责任。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are you tired of people asking you about donuts?
turns.zh: 您厌倦了别人问您关于甜甜圈的事了吗？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: I'll never get tired of it. Well, back when we met with people in person, people would bring me donuts, and I never got tired of it, nor did any of the people that I worked with who got to eat those donuts get tired of it. So, no, no, I'll never get tired of donuts.
turns.zh: 我永远都不会厌倦它。嗯，以前我们面对面开会时，人们会给我带甜甜圈，我从不厌倦吃甜甜圈，和我共事的那些有机会品尝甜甜圈的人也从不厌倦。所以，不，不，我永远都不会厌倦甜甜圈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Someone on Twitter asked what's a digital equivalent of bringing the donuts now that we're in a remote world. Do you have any advice on that?
turns.zh: 推特上有人问，现在处于远程办公时代，数字时代的"带甜甜圈"等同物是什么？你对此有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: That's a great question. I'm not even sure if the physical equivalent of donuts is donuts. I mean when I came up with that, I think it was really to be a metaphor around being a servant leader, bringing whatever needs to be done, filling the white space, filling the gaps, whatever needed to happen. So it doesn't always have to be donuts. (00:04:07): I did put that question out to some of the readers in my newsletter a while ago, maybe earlier in the pandemic, and got a lot of really interesting ideas. Maybe that was at a place where people had a little bit more patience for happy hours over Zoom and stuff like that. Maybe that patient set is worn out. The idea that I love the most was actual donuts. There was a PM who got DoorDash codes and found the best local donut place for each of the people on the team and basically sent them a code and said, "Click here and order the donuts to come to your house whenever you want them." So maybe at least partially the digital equivalent of donuts might be actual donuts.
turns.zh: 这是个很棒的问题。但我甚至不确定甜甜圈的物理对应物是否真的是甜甜圈。我想，当初我提出这个概念时，主要是想用它来比喻作为服务型领导者，随时做好需要做的事，填补空白，弥补缺失，完成需要完成的任务。所以不一定非得是甜甜圈。（00:04:07）：不久前，我在我的新闻通讯中向读者们提出了这个问题，可能是在疫情初期。当时人们对在Zoom上开欢乐时光之类活动还有点耐心。如今，可能那些有耐心的人已经疲惫了。我最喜欢的想法就是送真正的甜甜圈。有位产品经理拿到了DoorDash的优惠码，为团队里的每个人找到了当地最好的甜甜圈店，基本上就是给每个人发送一个代码，告诉他们：“点击这里，就能订购甜甜圈，随时送到你家。”所以，至少部分数字时代的“甜甜圈”可能就是实实在在的甜甜圈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Decentralized donuts.
turns.zh: 去中心化甜甜圈。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Decentralized donuts, on the blockchain.
turns.zh: 区块链上的去中心化甜甜圈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh boy, let's not go there.
turns.zh: 天哪，别扯这个了。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: I don't know what that is.
turns.zh: 我不知道那是什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I was perusing your career path ahead of this chat. You had this pretty wild career. You were an engineer initially, and then you were CTO at a part of NBC. Then you're a founder. Then you spent 14 years at Google working on products that folks may have heard of, like Google Docs and Google Calendar and Google Maps. You've also done a bunch of writing. Then more recently, you've become a full-time executive coach focusing on product people. (00:05:17): I have so many questions I'd love to ask you about your career and learnings along the way, and the writing. But I'd actually like to spend most of our time talking about the coaching and things that you've learned through that experience. And so, I have a couple questions just off the bat. What does an executive coach actually do? What kinds of things are you helping people with? What does a session look like? Then, two, just how did you decide you wanted to be a coach full time after leaving Google?
turns.zh: 在这次聊天前，我仔细研究了你的职业生涯。你有过一段相当丰富多彩的职业历程。最初你是一名工程师，后来在NBC旗下部门担任CTO，再后来成为创始人。你在谷歌工作了14年，参与开发了人们可能听说过的产品，比如Google Docs、Google Calendar和Google Maps。你还写了很多文章。最近，你成为了一名专注于产品人员的全职执行教练。（00:05:17）：我有很多问题想问你，关于你的职业生涯、一路走来的经验教训，还有写作部分。但我更想把大部分时间用来谈谈教练工作以及你从中获得的收获。那么，我先抛出几个问题。执行教练到底做些什么？你帮助人们解决哪些问题？一次咨询会是怎样的？然后，第二个问题：离开谷歌后，你为什么决定全职做教练？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah, that's a great question. I think coaching does mean a lot of different things. I mean it depends on who you talk to. It is a little bit of who you are, your style, your approach. Some people are calling themselves coaches, doing more mentoring, more advice. Other people are maybe more like me, more peer coaching. (00:06:01): To me, I see executive coaching as a partnership or creative partnership. It's all about helping my client reach their goals, their potential, whatever that means to them. So an important thing about coaching is the definition of success does belong to the client. I don't have an agenda. I don't have a set of things I'm trying to share, teach, learn. It really is fundamentally up to them, which means every client is completely different. They have different sense of where they want to go. Different barriers that might be standing in their way. (00:06:35): My coaching practice, I coach the whole person. So there is no restriction on what we might talk on, what we might work on together. It's not limited to product. It's not even limited to work or even leadership. It's wherever they want to go, whatever change, transformation means to them. (00:06:52): As coaches, we bring a bunch of tools to the conversation. The most important ones, honestly, are probably listening and curiosity, intuition, open-mindedness, really there to help challenge them to see things in different ways, help them tap into their imagination, figure out when there might be underlying beliefs, help them connect dots that need to be connected, help them disconnect things that feel connected. There's a lot of exploration to it. (00:07:20): It's very jazz-like. My love of jazz has been shared before, but there is an improvisation to it. What coaching is really powerful is you may not necessarily know where you're going when you start and you follow wherever there is meaning and change for that individual, wherever is they want to go. (00:07:38): The question around what brought me into it was actually interesting. I, honestly working with my own executive coach, started to figure out what it is that mattered to me, what I liked, what my values were, what my purpose was, started to unpack that I love deeply connecting with people and I love helping people change and grow. (00:08:01): The moments when I had the opportunity to do that as a manager, as a product leader were the most fulfilling parts of my career. And so, I started to unpack that and figure out what would it look like if that was what I did. (00:08:15): The other part of the journey was, for several years at Google, I worked at GV. It's Google Ventures, Google's venture capital arm. I had the opportunity to work with founders and product leaders in the portfolio. I started to simultaneously recognize the shortcomings of giving advice, because it seemed like, well, I can meet with these folks, I could tell them what I did, I could tell them what Google did, and that'll answer all their questions. (00:08:41): You start to realize advice is not as powerful as you might think it is. It's a little bit like cotton candy. Doesn't have a lot of nutrition. You get a nice sugar high. You feel great, both sides feel happy, but then a couple weeks later, a couple months later, nothing's really changed. (00:08:57): That's because it doesn't often confront the real problem. It often isn't relevant. Like what worked for us at Google may not have worked anywhere else. It may not even have worked at Google for all I know. I feel like there were years at Google where all we were doing was making things worse by showing up and we should just all have gone sat on a beach somewhere, and the company would've grown even faster. So who knows? (00:09:20): I mean so it was these just twin pillars of wanting to figure out where I could do what I like the most, and then also recognizing that where growth comes from is less around advice and telling people what to do and more about helping them figure out their own path, their own way. Then that ultimately you brought me into, hey, I want to do this full time, and that's what I've been doing ever since.
turns.zh:
是啊，这确实是个很棒的问题。我认为教练工作包含很多不同的含义。这取决于你与谁交流。它在一定程度上反映了你的个性、风格和方法。有些人自称教练，更多地提供指导和建议；而另一些人可能更像我，更多地进行同伴式辅导。（00:06:01）对我来说，高管教练是一种合作或创造性的伙伴关系。关键在于帮助客户实现他们的目标、挖掘他们的潜力，无论这对他们意味着什么。因此，成功的定义属于客户本人。这里没有既定议程。我不会试图分享、传授或学习特定内容。一切都由客户主导，这意味着每个客户都完全不同。他们对未来的期望各不相同，面临着不同的障碍和挑战。（00:06:35）在我的教练实践中，我会全方位关注客户。我们的对话不受任何限制，不局限于产品领域，甚至不局限于工作或领导力，而是涵盖他们想去的任何地方，以及对他们意义重大的任何改变。（00:06:52）作为教练，我们会带来一系列工具。说实话，最重要的可能是倾听、好奇心、直觉和开放心态，真正帮助客户以不同视角看问题，激发他们的想象力，识别潜在信念，帮助他们连接需要连接的点，拆解看似关联却实则割裂的认知。整个过程充满探索性。（00:07:20）这很像即兴爵士乐。我之前就分享过对爵士乐的热爱，但教练工作同样具有即兴特质。当你开始时不一定知道要去哪里，只要跟随对个人有意义和带来改变的方向，顺应他们的意愿即可。（00:07:38）探寻自己为何投身教练行业的过程很有趣。说实话，在与自己的高管教练合作时，我逐渐意识到对我重要的是什么——我的价值观、目标、与人深度连接的渴望，以及帮助他人成长的热情。（00:08:01）作为经理和产品负责人，能有机会践行这些理念的时刻，是我职业生涯中最充实的部分。于是我开始剖析，如果以此为职业会是什么样子。（00:08:15）旅程的另一部分是在谷歌的GV部门工作数年。我有机会与投资组合中的创始人和产品负责人合作。我逐渐意识到提供建议的效果并不如想象中强大。它有点像棉花糖，没有实质营养。短暂兴奋后，双方皆大欢喜，但几周、几个月后，一切如初。（00:08:57）这是因为建议往往未能触及核心问题，缺乏相关性。比如在谷歌行之有效的方法未必适用于其他地方，甚至在谷歌内部也未必普适。我在谷歌的那些年，我们做的大多是表面功夫。
我们的到场反倒让事情变得更糟。我们本该各自去海边晒晒太阳的，那样公司发展速度可能会更快。谁知道呢？（00:09:20）：我的意思是，这两大核心要素一是想找出自己最热爱做的事，二是意识到推动公司发展的关键不在于提供建议、指挥别人怎么做，而在于帮助他们找到自己的发展路径、找到属于自己的方法。最终这促使我下定决心——嘿，我想全职做这件事，从那以后我就一直这么做了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When do you find people come to you to get advice and coaching? What kind of clients do you find you end up working with?
turns.zh: 什么时候人们会来找你寻求建议和指导？你发现自己最终会与怎样的客户合作？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: That's a great question. Generally speaking, I work with senior product leaders, however you want to define that. Typically, these are chief product officers, VPs of product at startups, largely director level and above at bigger tech companies, some CEOs, other C-level execs in there. I think really anyone that considers themselves in a product leadership role. (00:10:15): Often they come to me because there's a career milestone or a crossroads, and it could be that they now find themselves in the position of being a CPO for the first time. Maybe there's a new industry change, or they've gone from a big company to a startup and a have this sense of what got me here isn't going to get me there. That's oftentimes when they reach out for coaching. (00:10:41): I think my clients are also very introspective and surrounded by great mentors and advisors and have all sorts of people in their life who can help them, but are realizing that a lot of the work is going to be internal work that's going to get them to the next level. And so, this transformation is going to be just as much what I need to do as who I am. That's often when people come to me.
turns.zh: 这是个很棒的问题。一般来说，我与高级产品领导者合作，无论你如何定义这个角色。通常，这些人包括首席产品官、初创公司的产品副总裁、大型科技公司的总监及以上级别，以及一些CEO和其他高管。我认为，只要自认为处于产品领导角色的人，都可能成为我的客户。（00:10:15）：他们来找我，往往是因为职业生涯的里程碑或十字路口。比如，他们可能首次担任首席产品官一职，又或许是从大公司转到初创公司，意识到过去的成功经验已无法助力他们更进一步。这些时刻往往是他们寻求指导的契机。（00:10:41）：我发现我的客户都非常善于自我反思，他们身边有优秀的导师和顾问，生活中也有各种能助他们一臂之力的人，但他们逐渐意识到，要想更上一层楼，关键在于自我突破。这场蜕变既关乎外界助力，也关乎内在修行。因此，当人们来找我时，往往带着这样的觉醒：他们需要改变的不仅是外部环境，更是自身的思维模式和行为习惯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You said that the way you coach is about the whole person. I'm curious ... I don't know if there's an answer to this, but when people come to get help and coaching, how much of their blocks, I guess, are rooted in their regular life versus skills, technical skills, and more like the PME, product leadership side, if that makes sense?
turns.zh: 你提到你的指导方式是关注人的整体状态。我很好奇……我不知道是否有标准答案，但当人们来寻求帮助和指导时，他们的阻碍因素中有多少源自日常生活，而非技能、技术能力或产品管理等专业领域？如果能理解我的意思的话。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah, I think ... Well, let me maybe try to illustrate this with an example from my life right now. Indulge me, I'm going to go a little bit left field here, but I promise [inaudible 00:11:45].
turns.zh: 嗯，让我用一个我现在生活中的例子来举例说明。请允许我稍微跑个题，但我保证[00:11:45的背景音被切断]。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 好的，开始吧。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: So we are teaching our 16-year-old son how to drive. So he just got his driver's permit. Do you remember when you learned how to drive, Lenny?
turns.zh: 所以我们正在教我们16岁的儿子开车。他刚拿到驾照。你还记得自己学车时的情景吗，莱尼？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I do. Yup.
turns.zh: 记得啊。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. So it's scary. I don't know if you know how your parents might have felt, but-
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。所以真的很吓人。不知道你父母当时的感受如何，但——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nope, [inaudible 00:12:06].
turns.zh: 不知道[00:12:06的背景音被切断]。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: ... [inaudible 00:12:06] on the other side of it. It's a whole new journey. Look, he's a smart kid. He's going to do great. But it helped me actually think back to when I learned how to drive. Actually, what I think is maybe a little bit more important here is before you learn to drive. And so, if you think about it as a ... When you're a kid, cars just go places. You get strapped in and you just wait and you get impatient. Then eventually you go somewhere. You're not even consciously aware of the concept of driving. Just cars just happen and you're not even aware of it. (00:12:41): As you get a little bit older, you start to become curious. You start to figure out, oh, that wheel has something to do with it. You turn the wheel. Maybe you start to understand there's pedals. But it also just seems really simple. Just like you get in the car and you drive it and you go somewhere. Maybe as you get older, you end up maybe even being a little bit of a smart Alec about how easy it looks and you start talking to your parents about, like, "It doesn't look hard. I can do this." (00:13:07): Now suddenly you're behind the wheel of the car. This is what my son is doing. Wow. Is it different than you thought it was going to be? Is it way more complicated? You have to remember check your mirrors. You've got to look before you turn. You didn't even know what that sign meant. You didn't know what those stripes meant. It is just overloading with complication and your internal mindset for confronting this challenge is not going to suit you the way you used to approach the world. (00:13:44): Maybe to put it in product leadership, product terms, everyone around you has got some real pithy advice about the things you're forgetting to do. It's like, "Hey, don't forget to check your mirror." Everyone's got a framework. It's like, "Ah, do you know about the 10:00 and 2:00 framework?" "Wait, what's the 10:00 and 2:00 framework?" "Oh, you just put your left hand on the 10:00, your right hand on the 2:00. That's the only thing you're missing. Here's a great medium post about that." Then you're like, "This is a problem is I have not adapted to the complexity of the world around me." (00:14:19): And so, there is this sense that what is interesting about driving is the world hasn't gotten any more complex. Driving's always been driving. But now your place in the world has shifted such that the internal meaning-making and self-complexity that is required requires a complete reboot of the internal operating system in order to allow you to thrive there. (00:14:41): And so, when you talk about this question of how much of this is skills, how much of this is tactics, how much of this is learning versus how much is internal growth, the answer is it's both, but the shift that is required is very much around how your inner self can make meaning and respond to the demands of the world around you so that you can succeed and thrive in this mindset shift that happens. (00:15:09): The skills matter, but by this point, you're beyond the place where you've learned the skills. There's mastering the skills, but there is this sense of what developmental psychologists call self-complexity, the ability to respond and adapt to that. (00:15:24): And so, I think we go through a lot of those shifts in our career. The driving example is simple. Actually, probably too simple, because the world is actually getting more complex for those of us that work in product. I mean every day something changes. It forces us to respond and adapt. So there aren't even rules of the road in product. (00:15:42): But I think this is what we're talking about, this question of the internal operating system I develop my ability to restructure it such that I can succeed given the demands that have been placed upon me.
turns.zh:
……[00:12:06的音频被截断]另一方面，这是一次全新的旅程。看，他是个聪明的孩子。他会做得很棒。但这让我回想起自己学车的时候。实际上，我认为更重要的是在学车之前的阶段。当你还是个孩子时，汽车只是载你去不同的地方。你被系好安全带，等着出发，然后变得不耐烦。最终你到了目的地，而你甚至没有意识到驾驶的概念。汽车就是自动行驶的，你对此毫无察觉。(00:12:41)：随着年龄增长，你开始变得好奇。你逐渐发现，比如方向盘和转向的关系。你转动方向盘。或许你开始明白还有踏板的存在。但这一切看起来依然简单。你上车开车，就能到达目的地。长大后，你甚至可能会对驾驶看似简单的过程沾沾自喜，对父母说：“这看起来不难，我能行。”(00:13:07)：但突然间，你坐在了驾驶座上。这就是我儿子正在经历的。哇。这和想象中的差别太大了吧？复杂得多得多！你得记得检查后视镜。转弯前要观察。那些标志的含义你根本不了解。那些标线又是什么意思？复杂的信息铺天盖地，面对这些挑战时，你原有的思维模式已然不适用了。(00:13:44)：用产品领导和产品术语来说，你身边每个人都会对你忘记做的事提出尖锐建议。比如，“别忘了检查后视镜。”每个人都有一套框架。比如，“你知道10点和2点的框架吗？” “等等，什么10点和2点的框架？” “哦，就是左手放在10点，右手放在2点。这就是你遗漏的关键。这里有篇关于这个的精彩中文文章。”然后你会意识到，“问题在于我没有适应周围世界的复杂性。”  (00:14:19)：所以，驾驶的趣味不在于世界变得更复杂了。驾驶始终是驾驶。但现在你的位置变了，内在的意义构建和自我成长的要求迫使你彻底重启内部操作系统，才能在这种思维转变中蓬勃发展。(00:14:41)：所以，当你讨论技能、战术、学习与内在成长的比例时，答案是两者兼备，但需要的转变在于你的内在自我如何解读世界，如何应对周围世界的需求，从而在这种思维转变中取得成功和成长。(00:15:09)：技能很重要，但到了这个阶段，你已经超越了学习技能的阶段。这是技能的精通阶段，但更重要的是发展心理学家所说的自我复杂性，即应对和适应环境的能力。(00:15:24)：所以，我们在职业生涯中会经历许多这样的转变。驾驶的例子很简单。事实上，可能太简单了，因为对我们从事产品工作的人来说，世界正变得越来越复杂。每天都有新变化，迫使我们应对和适应。因此，产品领域甚至没有通用的规则。
（00:15:42）：但我认为这正是我们所谈论的——这个关于内部操作系统的问题。我在不断提升自己的能力，以便能在面对各种挑战时成功达成目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What an amazing analogy. Totally hits home in a good and bad way. It's a really good segue to something I wanted to chat about, something that we talked about before the recording, which is what you're finding to be one of the bigger unlocks for your clients. It's also a concept that you've been spending a lot of time refining and you're finding is helping people shift, and specifically shift their leadership mindset. And so, I'd love to just hear you talk through your thinking there.
turns.zh: 多么绝妙的比喻啊！无论是从积极还是消极的角度来看，都说到了点子上。这个比喻正好能引出我接下来想聊的话题——这是我们录制前就讨论过的，也是你们发现对客户最具启发性的突破之一。这个概念也是你花了大量时间精心打磨的，而且你发现它能帮助人们转变思维，尤其是转变他们的领导思维模式。所以，我很想听听你对此的深入思考。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah, it does sort lead into this. Maybe another analogy that might work for your listeners, if you think about product management, your career arc and where you are challenged from a mindset perspective, in some ways it does feel like the early part of your career. You're learning to play a video game. Hopefully there's a tutorial. Your first job is learning the ropes, somebody's teaching you. You maybe have managers that are giving you simple little missions that you can succeed at and if you fail, the consequences aren't bad. (00:17:03): It does feel like a little bit ... And I felt this way, and I talked to a lot of people earlier in their career. It does feel like you're trying to learn the rules of the game, trying to figure out the physics. You want to run up the score. (00:17:15): You get better at playing the game. You fail, but you start to develop some confidence that when you fail, you'll learn from it. You'll get better. You get really good at the game. You get promoted, you get rewarded, you unlock new levels, teach other people how to play the game. You start to feel really awesome about yourself. (00:17:32): But then suddenly you're put in a place where you realize that the rules of the game aren't so black and white. Maybe there's a long delay now between when you get to see what you did and the score of it. Things start to behave in unexpected ways. The physics start to get weird. You're on a level where you're floating. I don't know what the right metaphor is here. (00:17:52): But you start to recognize that there's been this huge change. The most frightening part about it is you look around and everyone is looking at you like you're the designer of the game, and you thought you were playing. That's often what it feels like when you move into a leadership role, to come back to this sense of what got me here is not going to get me there. (00:18:17): I work with a lot of leaders and sometimes that's come with a pretty significant cost, this juxtaposition, maybe your happiness, your health, your marriage. There's been this existential crisis of I don't know if I love this anymore. Maybe it leads to burnout. Maybe it's not even that dire. It's just a sense of, well, I'm looking around and I need to be something. I need to unlock something else to continue on this path. There is a sense of stuckness that comes from that. (00:18:45): What I've come to realize is this is the precipice of, I think, this pretty fundamental concept in leadership. I'm not the originator of this, so this has come up again and again and again. It's not new. It's going to sound familiar. It's like the flood myth from Gilgamesh showing up in all this oral histories of the world. It's not new. (00:19:10): Conscious Leadership Group, an organization that I'm big fan of, they call it above the line versus below the line. Brene Brown calls it daring versus armored leadership, sage versus warrior. Even in the world of sports, there's playing to win versus playing not to lose. It's this concept that's come up again and again. Leadership Circle calls it creative versus reactive, and that's the term I'm going to use. I like that. (00:19:35): Here's the distinction. Very simple. Are you responding to the world from a place of fear, where you see problems and threats, you want to be right, you want to be liked, you're defensive as an inward approach, or are you responding to the world from a place of openness, possibility, curiosity, passion, growth, purpose? Very simple concept. Pretty much everyone understands what I mean. It makes sense. (00:20:11): Everyone also then immediately says a couple of different things. "That sounds amazing. I'd rather have that," or, "Here are moments when I've felt that," but that's usually followed up by a couple of questions. "I don't know if that works. It doesn't sound very effective. Is it possible?" Then how do you that? (00:20:38): The effective part is actually a question we can answer, which is, yes, it is more effective. Bob Anderson, Bill Adams are two management scientists who've written extensively, done a whole bunch of research, and they have looked at every possible dimension you can imagine of success, both leadership capability, they've looked at revenue, brand, profitability, everything, and it's shown, yes, this creative form of leadership is in every possible way positively correlated with success and reactive leadership is negatively correlated. So, yes, it works yet. (00:21:17): Yet, according to their research, some 75% of leaders are primarily operating reactively. So most leaders are operating from a place of fear, reacting, seeing problems, and threats. That's because that other question of how do you do it is such a hard one to answer. It's not an easy thing that you flip the switch of. It goes back to this notion of redesigning that internal operating system, so how you confront the world, what underlying belief systems and assumptions you have that are causing you to operate from that place.
turns.zh:
是的，这确实引出了这个话题。或许用另一个比喻能让听众更容易理解——如果你想想产品管理，你的职业发展轨迹，以及你从思维角度面临挑战的部分，在某种程度上，确实感觉像是职业生涯的早期阶段。你在学习玩一款游戏。希望有教程指导。你的第一份工作就是熟悉规则，有人教你入门。你的上司可能会布置一些你能成功完成的小任务，如果失败了，后果也不算太严重。（00:17:03）：确实感觉有点……我自己也曾有过这种感受，也和许多处于职业生涯早期的人聊过。这确实像是在学习游戏规则，试图弄清楚其中的物理法则。你想不断提高得分。
（00:17:15）：你会逐渐掌握游戏技巧。失败后，你开始建立信心，相信失败后能从中学习并进步。最终你变得非常擅长游戏，获得晋升和奖励，解锁新关卡，还能教别人玩游戏。这时你会自我感觉良好。（00:17:32）：但突然间，你会发现游戏规则不再那么黑白分明。现在你完成操作后要等很久才能看到结果，游戏机制开始变得不可预测。物理法则变得异常。现在你在悬浮层。我不知道该用什么比喻来形容。（00:17:52）：但你开始意识到发生了巨大的变化。最令人恐惧的是，你环顾四周，发现每个人都把你当成游戏设计师，而你以为自己只是个玩家。这就是进入领导角色时最常见的感受——过去的经验不再适用。
（00:18:17）：我和许多领导者合作过，有时这会带来巨大的代价——这种认知冲突可能会影响你的幸福感、健康状况和婚姻关系。这是一种存在主义危机——我不知道自己是否还热爱这份工作。也许这会导致职业倦怠，也许没那么严重。但你会感到迷茫，需要找到新的方向继续前进。这里有一种停滞感。
（00:18:45）：我意识到，这正是领导力中一个相当基础的概念的临界点。这个概念并非我首创，它一次又一次被提及，并非新鲜事物。你听起来会觉得熟悉。比如吉尔伽美什的洪水神话，在世界各地的口述历史中都能找到踪影。它由来已久。
（00:19:10）：我非常推崇的Conscious Leadership Group将其称为"线上"与"线下"。布琳·布朗称之为"勇敢型领导"与"盔甲型领导"，"智者"与"斗士"。甚至在体育界，也有"为赢而战"与"不输则赢"的区别。这个概念一次又一次被提及。Leadership Circle称之为"创造性"与"反应性"，我更喜欢这个术语。
（00:19:35）：区别很简单。你是出于恐惧应对世界——看到问题和威胁，急于证明自己，渴望被喜欢，采取防御姿态；还是出于开放、可能性、新奇、激情、成长和使命感去应对世界？这个概念很简单。几乎所有人都懂我的意思。这很合理。
（00:20:11）：
随后，每个人都会立即说出几句不同的看法。比如：“这听起来太棒了。我宁愿选择那样。”或者：“我也有过类似的感受。”但紧接着通常会抛出几个疑问：“我不确定这是否可行。听起来效果不明显。真的能行吗？”那么具体该怎么做呢？（00:20:38）  
实际上，答案是肯定的。两位管理学者鲍勃·安德森和比尔·亚当斯通过大量研究表明，创造性领导力与成功存在正相关，而被动式领导力则与成功呈负相关。他们研究了成功的各个维度，包括领导能力、营收、品牌、盈利能力等方方面面，都证实了这一结论。（00:21:17）  
然而，根据他们的研究，约75%的领导者主要采取被动式领导方式。这意味着大多数领导者都处于恐惧应对的状态——不断应对问题，识别威胁。这是因为如何做到这一点实在太难了。这绝非简单地按下开关就能实现的问题。关键在于重塑内部运作系统——即如何看待世界，以及你所秉持的哪些潜在信念和假设正导致你陷入被动应对的境地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can I ask you a quick question? Just to clarify the two sides, what's a sign that you're in the reactive side of things? I think one thing you said is you're worrying a lot about how people think about you and make sure that they like you. Is there anything else that's going to tell a listener, "Oh, maybe I'm falling into this trap"?
turns.zh: 我能问你个小问题吗？想帮你理清两方面的区别。怎样判断自己正处于被动应对的状态？我记得你提到过，你总是很担心别人对你的看法，还总想确保别人喜欢你。有没有其他迹象能让听众一听就明白：“哦，也许我也陷入了这种陷阱？”

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah, you've nailed it, which is that fear, like operating from a place of anxiety. There are different ways, depending on our mindsets, our approaches. I like the word postures because it seems to click different ways that we retreat into this reactive mode. Fear and anxiety is the way. That's how you know. You're just like, "Ugh, I'm below the line." I'm just like I'm seeing problems. I'm seeing threats. (00:22:43): Our brains are hardwired to do that, so it's not like that's wrong. These are brains that learn to do that, I don't know, on the tundra being chased by wild animals. So this is our normal way of being. There might be different desires and needs that force you to operate that way. We think there's really three of these postures. (00:23:11): Anybody is probably more than one of them, so this is not pathologizing. This isn't putting you in a box. But probably one of these will resonate more than the others. Wanting to be approved, wanting to be loved, wanting other people to like you. This was me in my early part of my career.
turns.zh: 没错，你说得很到位，就是恐惧心理——比如总是处于焦虑的状态。根据我们的思维模式和行为方式，会有不同的表现方式。我特别喜欢“姿态”这个词，因为它能很好地解释我们陷入被动应对模式的不同原因。恐惧和焦虑就是典型例子。当你意识到自己正处于这种状态时，就会觉得：“天哪，我已经跌破底线了。”比如总是在看到问题、察觉威胁的时候。（00:22:43）：我们的大脑天生就设定了这种应对机制，所以这并不可耻。这种大脑机制可以追溯到远古时期，比如在冻原上被野生动物追逐时。这种反应模式是我们与生俱来的。可能还有其他欲望和需求迫使你采用这种应对方式。我们认为有三种典型的应对姿态。（00:23:11）：每个人很可能不止有一种姿态，所以这并非在病态化你，也不是把你框死。但其中总有一两种姿态会比其他更能引起共鸣。比如渴望被认可、渴望被爱、渴望让别人喜欢你。这就是我职业生涯早期的状态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Same.
turns.zh: 我也一样。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah. So you're kind of like the heart type. It's sometimes called move toward other people. A lot of that came from my environment. I was coming up with product management. No one necessarily knew what the job even was. I had no authority and most people could just ignore me if they wanted to. And so, I had to meet other people's expectations, please them, want to be accepted by them, seek their approval. It was this what we call a complying approach. (00:23:58): Here, this is why this is so vexing is it actually worked really well. It was pretty effective. Other people liked working with me. I listened to them and I considered everyone's needs and made sure everyone felt heard. But there came a point where I gave away so much power that it was hurting me when it came to purpose and execution and decisiveness. (00:24:22): And so, again, these aren't bad. There's usually underlying tendencies that are very good. It just starts to have a cost as you become more senior. It's like the gears start to grind to a halt a little bit. (00:24:35): Another way is more of a needing to be right head type, protecting one's own ideas, sometimes called a move away from type, distance, arrogance, criticism, retreating into your own ideas and head. Then the other will not be a surprise, is the more controlling, my way or the highway, autocratic will move against wanting to win, wanting to be number one, wanting to excel, wanting dominance, wanting control, this would be another tendency. (00:25:10): Often one of those feels natural to you and another one feels just so incredibly distasteful that you can't imagine possibly operating that way. This goes into the underlying beliefs part. If you had told me early in my career, when you saw me being passive and people-pleasing like that, "You've just got to stop caring what other people think, Ken. You've got to be more pushy." (00:25:41): People did say that to me. That was pretty common probably in my performance review. It was very common. Even people who worked for me were like, "You need to push back." My only archetype for doing that was the autocratic, controlling type. I was like, "I don't want to be like that. That guy's a jerk. That's a fascist. I don't want to be a fascist. I do care about other people." (00:26:04): And so, many of our examples and archetypes are these equally ineffective reactive ways of being. And so, no wonder I didn't want to be like that, because that's also not very effective either. But there was a sense for me of redefining ... This is where coaching is powerful is this what are the underlying assumptions and beliefs that you have that are causing you to fall back on some of these fundamental ways of operating and not let go of them? (00:26:35): Because the answer for me wasn't stop caring about other people. I wasn't going to do that. That's a value of mine. It's part of who I am. But take the caring about other people, the empathy, the connection, and direct it in a more creative way where you're operating now from a place of purpose and vision and not reacting and protecting and defending and wanting to be. (00:26:56): For me, the key to that was letting go of needing to be liked and redefining it as an admiration that takes place over time. So rather than I want to leave this room with everyone liking me, I started to realize I want to be the type of leader where, a decade later, people say, "I would work with that guy again in a heartbeat." That was part of the unlock for me. (00:27:25): Again, I care about other people. That's a natural gift that underlines it. But it's a redefinition of how that serves me, if that makes sense.
turns.zh:
是啊。所以你属于那种以他人为中心的人格类型。这种类型有时被称为"迎合他人"。这种性格特质很大程度上源于我的成长环境。我最初从事产品管理工作时，没人真正了解这个职位的职责。我没有任何权威地位，人们可以随意忽视我的意见。因此，我不得不迎合他人的期望，讨好他们，寻求他们的认可。这就是我们所说的"顺从型"策略。（00:23:58）：这里最令人困惑的是，这种策略其实效果不错。它相当有效，其他人喜欢与我共事。我倾听他们的意见，考虑每个人的需求，确保每个人都能被倾听。但到了一定程度，我让渡了太多权力，以至于这在目标设定、执行力和果断决策方面对我产生了负面影响。（00:24:22）：所以，再说一次，这些性格特质本身并无过错。通常背后都有积极的潜在倾向。但当你职位越高时，这种倾向就会产生代价。就像齿轮开始慢慢卡住。（00:24:35）：另一种倾向是需要证明自己正确，固守己见，有时被称为"疏远型"。这种人会拒绝听取他人的意见，退缩到自己的世界里。与之相反的倾向则是控制欲强、独断专横、以自我为中心，渴望掌控局面、追求胜利、争夺头把交椅。（00:25:10）：通常其中一种性格特质对你来说顺其自然，而另一种则令人深恶痛疾，难以想象自己会以那种方式行事。这就涉及到深层信念层面了。如果在职业生涯早期，有人对我说："你别在乎别人怎么想，肯恩。你得更有主见些。"（00:25:41）：确实有人这么对我说。这种评价在我的绩效评估中很常见。甚至我的下属也会说："你得反击。"我唯一能模仿的领导类型就是独断专横的那种。我会说："我不想那样做。那家伙是个混蛋。是个法西斯。我不想当法西斯。我在乎别人的。"（00:26:04）：因此，我们看到的许多例子和原型都是同样低效的被动应对方式。难怪我不愿成为那样的人，因为那样的做法同样无效。但对我来说，关键在于重新定义……教练指导的价值在于，帮助你审视那些导致你固守这些基本应对方式、无法放手的潜在假设和信念。（00:26:35）：对我来说，答案不是停止在乎他人。我不会那样做。这是我的价值观，也是我本质的一部分。但要把在乎他人转化为创造性的表达方式，让你的行动源于目标和愿景，而非被动反应、自我保护和争强好胜。（00:26:56）：对我来说，关键在于放下被他人认可的需求，重新定义这种需求为一种随着时间推移而形成的赞赏。于是，我不再执着于离开会议时所有人都喜欢我，而是开始意识到，我要成为那种十年后人们会说："我会毫不犹豫地再次与他共事"的领导者。这对我来说就是突破的关键。（00:27:25）：再说一次，我在乎他人。这是支撑这一切的天赋。但
这是对它如何为我服务的一种重新定义，如果你能理解的话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Say someone's in that first bucket ... And I was definitely in that first bucket. I still want people to like me and I still probably have flaws there. But say you're a PM and you're like, "Oh, man. That's exactly how I am acting right now." It sounds like is the core of it just a mindset shift, going from I need people to like me to what you just talked about of, okay, I'm going to shift to I just want them to respect me over time? Is that the core of it? I know it's probably not that easy, but how should someone behave during that bucket right now?
turns.zh: 假设有人处于第一个思维框架中……而我过去确实深陷其中。我依然渴望被他人认可，可能仍存在缺点。但假设你是一位项目经理，突然意识到：“天啊，我现在就是这样行事的。” 这听起来关键在于思维模式的转变——从渴望被喜欢转向追求尊重。核心问题在于如何实现这种转变？我知道这并不容易，但当你身处这个框架中时，该如何自处？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah. It sounds easy, right? This is part of what's hard about this, is it always sounds easy when you describe it, having gone through the journey. It's sort of like talk to somebody on the summit of Mount Everest and they'll be like, "Yeah. Well, I could just climb this mountain. That's how I got here." You're like, "Okay, wait, that's not that easy." Again, it is very individualized. (00:28:21): I think there's an appreciation that you have to understand what is holding you back. This is a lot of the work that I'll do with my clients is what is those underlying expectations? What are these underlying beliefs? (00:28:40): I Believe that my style was incompatible with being the leader. I would've said I can't be a CEO because I'm not tough enough. I'm not strong enough. I'm not commanding enough. I can't command a room. It's like, okay, what is the underlying belief I'm making about what leadership is there? There's an archetype that I have in my mind that is incompatible with this this way. (00:29:10): And so, there's a need to confront that. Okay, what makes you believe the only type of leader is the leader that orders people around? Maybe that's all I've ever seen. Maybe I don't believe it's possible to be another type of leader. Maybe there's an inner critic that is convincing me that that's not who I am, because a part of it is redefinition of what does leadership need for you, for you authentically? What would it be like, in my case, to lead with purpose and be decisive and lead with vision and to have other people felt like they're being brought along and listened to and participated and create safe spaces for other people? That was the question there. (00:29:47): It took people challenging my point of view. It took working with a coach, asking me questions, forcing me to see places I'd made connections, that the connections don't really need to be made. There's a lot of instruments and tools we work with in coaching. There's 360-degree assessments that are very helpful here that will start to help you understand, hey, here are places where you're operating actively. Here are places where you're operating really creatively, because, by the way, most people are partially somewhere in that journey. It's a developmental process. (00:30:17): And to start to be able to get the feedback, the dopamine hit of seeing when I do it this way, actually it's more effective and it doesn't cost me as much. I'm happier and I'm enjoying it, I'm seeing that it's working, is oftentimes a big part of this because there is this belief that it won't work. The number of times when I'm with a client in coaching and say, "Well, what if you did do that?" and they go, "It just won't work." You realize that there is this wiring in there that needs ... And this is what I talk about, this operating system that needs to be rejiggered to start to make sense of what if it did and how might you know.
turns.zh: 是啊，这听起来很简单，对吧？但实际操作时却难上加难。就像攀登珠峰的人说得轻巧：“嗯，我只要爬上这座山就行了。”你会说：“等等，这可没那么容易。” 这完全因人而异。（00:28:21）我认为关键在于理解阻碍自己的因素。这正是我与客户合作的核心——那些潜在的期望是什么？深层的信念又是什么？（00:28:40）我曾坚信自己的领导风格与领导者身份不符。比如我会说：“我当不了CEO，因为我不够强硬，不够果断，缺乏指挥力。” 但真正的问题在于，我对领导者的定义与现实存在偏差。（00:29:10）所以必须直面这些认知。为什么你认为领导者必须高高在上？或许这是我见过的唯一领导模式。或许我不相信存在其他领导类型。或许内心的自我批判告诉我这不是真实的自己，因为这需要重新定义什么才是真正适合你的领导力？对我而言，如何以目标为导向、果断决策、远见卓识，同时让团队成员感受到被重视、被倾听、被赋能，并为他们创造安全的环境，这才是关键。（00:29:47）这需要他人挑战我的固有观念，需要教练的引导，需要剖析自身的思维模式。教练会用360度评估工具帮助我认识到：有些行为看似自然，实则无需刻意维持。多数人在成长过程中都深陷某个思维框架中，这是一个持续发展的过程。（00:30:17）而获得反馈后的多巴胺激增——当你发现以某种方式行事更高效、更省心时，幸福感油然而生，这正是突破固有认知的关键。太多客户在教练过程中说：“试试这样做吧。”得到的回应却是“不行，这永远行不通。” 这说明他们内心深处的信念需要重塑，需要重装操作系统，才能理解假设的可能性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The point you just made about how you can realize that you can be successful in a lot of different ways and you don't have to be this one archetype of a leader really resonates with my experience. I actually had an executive coach for a few months, and that was probably the biggest unlock for me. We did the strengths exercise, which a lot of people do. The main thing that she helped me see is you can do all the things that you want to do through the lens of the strengths that you have and not have to force yourself to be good at these other things, because there's many ways to accomplish the same outcomes.
turns.zh: 你刚才提到的观点，即你可以意识到自己可以通过多种方式取得成功，而不必非要成为某种领导力刻板印象中的典型人物，这真的让我深有共鸣。实际上，我曾请过一位高管教练指导了几个月，这对我来说可能是最重要的启发。我们做过很多人的都会做的“优势识别”练习。但她让我意识到最重要的一点是，你可以通过发挥自身优势来达成所有想要实现的目标，而不必强迫自己去擅长其他领域的事，因为实现相同目标的途径其实有很多。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: That's exactly right. Then once you start to understand that, you start to develop a better way of finding the right place, the right environment, the right role. When we began the conversation, you asked me what brought me into executive coaching. I would feel these ... I would describe it as flying too close to the sun in my career, where I would have a team. I'd be managing a small team. I would love it. I would enjoy it. Then suddenly my team would grow. (00:31:57): I'd become more senior than I felt comfortable being. Then I felt like I wasn't getting to do the "real" work anymore. Then I would be just completely disheveled and dissatisfied. Then I'd go try to go find a smaller team or even stop being a manager. It was a very meandering, reactive path. It was like every so often I was catching a wave, and I knew what it felt like to be on the wave, but I didn't know what the characteristics of the wave were. (00:32:23): Then through coaching, I was like I love connecting with other people. I like helping people grow. I like helping challenge people. I like helping. Then I was like what are those parts? What if I unpack those? Oh, that's why I loved managing that team of five because I got to do a lot of it. That's why I hated managing a team of 35 because there's no time for it. (00:32:44): Then you start to say, okay, well, what if rather than just randomly meandering through my career, I actually elevated needing to connect, wanting to be helpful? Then you're like what would it be like if I wanted the helping professions? It's just a reframing of move through your career in a way that seems externally to fit some definition of success and to start to define that internally. (00:33:11): That is the very definition of the reactive versus creative mindset. Reactive, allowing the world to set the expectations and try to meet them versus tap into what your real, true sense of purpose and vision is. Then use that to navigate the world.
turns.zh:
没错。等你意识到这一点后，你就能更好地找到适合自己的职位、环境和角色。刚开始聊起这个话题时，你问我是什么促使我投身高管教练领域。我可以说，我在职业生涯中曾多次“贪大求全”，比如管理一个小团队时，我乐在其中，可突然团队规模扩大后，我发现自己超出了舒适区，无法再专注于“核心工作”。那时我变得焦虑不安，甚至考虑换个小团队或彻底放弃管理职位。这条职业道路可谓曲折坎坷，每次碰到机遇，我都兴奋不已，却从未深刻理解机遇的本质。

透过教练训练，我逐渐发现自己热爱与人建立联结、助力他人成长、激发挑战的能力。然后我追问：这些特质从何而来？如何深挖内核？原来我曾热爱管理五人团队，是因为能深度参与每个环节；而管理35人团队则因精力不足而心生倦怠。（00:32:44）于是我开始思考：与其随波浮沉，不如主动提升连接他人、助人成长的能力？若投身帮助型职业会怎样？这不过是以不同视角审视职业生涯：既顺应外界对成功的定义，又从内而外定义自我价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting that so much of this is just mindset. It's not like learning a new skill as a leader or a product manager. It's just seeing yourself in the world differently. All of a sudden you unlock your career. Is that what you find?
turns.zh: 有趣的是，很多问题的核心在于思维模式转变。这与学习新技能或管理技能不同，关键在于以不同视角审视自我，进而解锁职业潜能。你认同吗？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Absolutely. That's why I think so much of the focus on the skills, the frameworks, it can be limited as you develop these capabilities, because it's inner work. Where we're talking about is this is all me. (00:33:57): Now that's empowering. There's empowerment to be able to say I want to change something and it doesn't involve a whole bunch of other people convincing and persuading them, getting into an executive ... This is all me. But it also, in some ways, makes it harder because it is all you. In coaching, it's all about you. It's all about that. Who am I and what matters to me? What underlying belief systems, inner voices are challenging me in ways that I want to be challenged? What is my unique ... (00:34:31): I love the word authenticity. It's, like you were just talking about, like what is my authentic way to lead, and then how do I center that rather than trying to fit into someone else's definition of what leadership might be? (00:34:43): You may recognize I can't be that authentic way of leader at this place or in this place type of company, but I know how to find it and I'm going to go find it.
turns.zh: 绝对是这样。这就是为什么我非常重视技能和框架的学习，但随着你不断提升这些能力，这种学习可能会逐渐失去意义，因为这需要从内而外的修炼。我们所谈论的，完全是关于个人的成长。（00:33:57）：现在这很赋能。能够说我想改变某件事，而不需要依赖他人来说服和说服他们，参与高管层……这一切都取决于我自己。但从某种程度上说，这也让事情变得更难了，因为一切都取决于你自己。教练指导的核心就是关注你自己——你是谁？什么对你最重要？哪些潜在的信念体系和内在的声音正在挑战你？你独特的……（00:34:31）：我喜欢“真实性”这个词。正如你刚才所说，这关乎我如何以真实的方式领导，然后如何以此为核心，而不是试图去迎合别人对领导力的定义？（00:34:43）：你可能会意识到，在某些地方或某些类型的公司，我无法成为那种真实的领导者，但我知道如何找到它，并且我会去找到它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have any more examples of either someone uncovering this about themselves, or another mindset shift that you can make in one of these other buckets, similar to the idea of I'll think about people over the long term versus immediately?
turns.zh: 你有没有更多例子，比如有人发现自己的这一面，或者在其他方面也有类似的思维转变，比如从短期考虑他人到长期考虑他人？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah. It really does vary. You start to pick up on that shift when it's less of the goals being defined externally and more of the goals being defined internally. So you'll have a conversation with somebody who's new to coaching and you'll say, "What do you want?" They'll be like, "Well, I want to get promoted to VP." "Why?" "Because I want to be a VP." It's like, "Well, what's important about being VP?" "Well, because ... " Eventually the answer is, well, because it's there and that's the thing that I'm supposed to do. (00:35:45): Then you start to notice the shift and it starts to become more of, "Well, because really what's important to me is creativity. I want more creativity in my life. I want more ability to challenge other people." And so, you start to just sense that's more from in than from out. That's where that shift is. (00:36:06): The journey is different for everyone. I think ultimately this is part of why, quite frankly, coaching may not be right for everyone. If we go back to that video game analogy, if you're looking for someone to just teach you the tutorial so you can learn how to play the video game and there's this jackass like me sitting next to you and saying, "What's important to you about playing this video game?" you're going to be like, "Just can you tell me how to hold the controller? Can you stop?" (00:36:31): So it's not always right. It's a place where I think oftentimes people recognize that they've gotten all the advice, all the frameworks, all the rules, all the tricks, all the tips. They've learned that, they've mastered it, they've tweaked it, they've optimized it, they've recognized the shortcomings, they've customized it. The emergence that's required for them to get to the next level is just going to come just as much from inside them as it is from outside, if not more. That's when that shift is made.
turns.zh: 是的。这确实因人而异。当目标不再由外部定义，而是由内部定义时，你就能察觉到这种转变。比如你和一个刚接触教练的人交谈，你会问：“你想要什么？”他们可能会说：“嗯，我想升职到副总裁。”“为什么？”“因为我想当副总裁。”你会问：“那当副总裁对你来说重要吗？”他们会说：“嗯，因为……” 最终答案是，因为这是别人期望我做的，而不是我真正想做的。（00:35:45）：然后你开始注意到这种转变，更多地转向：“嗯，因为对我来说，真正重要的是创造力。我希望生活中有更多的创造力，我希望有更多挑战他人的能力。”所以，你会意识到这更多地来自内心而非外部。这就是转变所在。（00:36:06）：每个人的旅程都不同。我认为最终这就是为什么，坦白说，教练可能并不适合每个人。如果用电子游戏来打比方，如果你找个人只教你教程，让你学会怎么玩游戏，而旁边有个像我这样的混蛋，说：“对你来说，玩这个游戏重要的是什么？”你可能会说：“能不能告诉我怎么握住控制器？能不能闭嘴？” （00:36:31）：所以这并不总是正确的做法。在我看来，通常人们会意识到，他们已经获得了所有的建议、框架、规则、技巧。他们已经掌握了这些，调整了它们，优化了它们，认识到了不足之处，并进行了定制。要想更上一层楼，所需的突破必须来自内心，甚至更多地来自内心。那时，转变就会发生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's called mentorship, I think, for people that are just looking for actual concrete advice on how to do a thing, is that right, versus coaching?
turns.zh: 对于那些只想获得如何做某事的具体建议的人来说，这叫做导师指导，对吧？而教练指导呢？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: I think so. This is where the words are squishy because there are a lot of people who are mentoring, who are also stepping into a coach role occasionally. There are plenty of managers who are great at coaching as necessary. So skills run the gamut, but it's a question of how much are you looking for someone to tell you the right way versus how much do you believe that there even is no right way? It's ultimately going to have to be your way. (00:37:33): That's a different place, a different point in your career at different levels of journey. It's part of why I tend to work with probably more senior executives, because they're not looking to me to tell them how to do the job. They've already learned how to do the job. It's just something deeper that's going to need to break through from that.
turns.zh:
我觉得是这样的。这里之所以会出现模糊不清的情况，是因为有很多导师在指导他人时，偶尔也会扮演教练的角色。还有很多管理者在必要时也很擅长进行指导。因此，技能水平参差不齐，但关键在于，你是希望别人告诉你正确的做法，还是认为根本不存在所谓的正确方法？最终，答案必须符合你的实际情况。

（00:37:33）：这涉及到不同职业阶段、不同发展阶段的不同境遇。这也是我为何更倾向于与资深高管合作的原因之一，因为他们不需要我来告诉他们如何开展工作。他们早已掌握了这些技能。真正需要突破的，是更深层次的思维模式。
