turns.zh:
本期节目由Unit赞助。Gusto、Uber、Shopify和AngelList有什么共同点？它们都决定将银行服务整合到自己的产品中。据AngelList产品负责人称："银行服务让每个功能都更具吸引力。有了它，我们的平台就能为客户提供财务管理的核心支持；没有它，我们不过是堆积如山的软件工具中的一员。"

（00:38:12）：将银行服务嵌入产品不仅能提升差异化，还能帮助你获取、留住并变现客户。Unit是银行即服务领域的市场领导者，整合多家银行合作伙伴与开发者友好型API，让各种规模的企业都能在数周内上线账户、卡片、支付和借贷功能。

（00:38:33）：Unit已获得AngelList、Highbeam、Invoice2go和Roofstock等头部品牌的信任。若想了解Unit如何助力像您这样的企业构建银行服务，欢迎访问unit.co/lenny申请演示或体验免费沙盒。网址是unit.co/lenny。

（00:38:51）：对于那些想努力提升但找不到教练、又负担不起教练费用的人，有没有什么自学方法能帮助他们转变思维模式、完成您所描述的诸多任务？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah, it's a great question. Here's the secret about the coaching industry. Anyone can call themselves a coach. It's very democratized. It's great. There's no gatekeepers and barriers and there's no 500 licenses you have to go through. (00:39:22): There are tons of great coaches who are at various different price levels, at different levels of accessibility. And so, if you say, "I can't afford a coach," I might challenge that a little bit and say have you looked? (00:39:36): The other thing is that you don't need a coach who's done the job before. I mean obviously I've done the job before, so I'm undermining part of my own selling point here. But coaches are trained to coach people on any topic. So when I go through coach training, I can coach you on anything. People can coach you on anything. (00:39:52): Sometimes even there might be power in having a coach that's never done the product management job because there won't be any cheating of starting to move into a more of advisor role or maybe as the coach either. There may be, "Well, you tell me what should I should do," and the person would be like, "I don't know. I've never done this job. Let's go back to what you want." So there could be some benefit from that. Again, you don't have to have done that. (00:40:13): So I would say coaching is incredibly powerful. I wish I'd had a coach much, much earlier in my career. And so, the answer may be coaching is more accessible than you thought. If not, I think the things that we're talking about here are internal understanding of what matters to you, your sense of purpose, this inner curiosity, and that could be harnessed at any age. So just wondering about yourself at any point in your career, wondering what's important to you. (00:40:43): I love doing values work, like, "What are your values? Okay. No. What really are your values?" That's something you can do yourself. That's something you can question. You can read about, you can start to understand. (00:40:53): Mentors can be great, especially mentors who are less about trying to tell you the right way and get you to follow directly their path, but are more they're applying some curiosity, asking questions, challenging you in certain ways, being a way that you can bounce ideas off of. (00:41:09): Great managers, I think, especially the best product leaders, understand how to put the coach hat on and when it's appropriate to put the coach hat on, and are explicit about that, are like, "Okay, let me take off my manager hat now and put the coach hat on. What do you really want to do, Lenny? What's important to you? What's your career?" And so, I think you can get coaching from everywhere. (00:41:28): There's a lot of self-coaching you can do. This is honestly one of the benefits for me having gone through tons of training and coaching is starting to coach myself, like feeling an emotion and asking myself coach questions. Really powerful. That's something you can do when you've had a coach. You can do it when you don't have a coach. You can explore it. (00:41:46): So I think this is really all about really being curious and wanting to understand who you really are at the core and what's important to you and what matters. That's something that can be done with or without a coach.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实是个好问题。关于教练行业的秘密在于，任何人都能自称教练。这行业非常民主化，这很棒。没有行业门槛和限制，也无需通过繁琐的认证流程。（00:39:22）：市场上有很多优秀的教练，他们的价格各异，服务的可及性也不同。比如你说“我请不起教练”，我可能会反问一句：“你真的找过了吗？”（00:39:36）：另外，你不需要找曾从事过相关工作的教练。当然我自己就曾从业过，所以这里多少有点自卖自夸。不过教练接受过专业训练，可以指导人们处理任何议题。例如，我接受教练培训后，就能为你提供任何领域的指导。任何人都能为你提供指导。（00:39:52）：有时候，让没有产品管理经验的教练指导你，反而能带来优势——因为他们不会假装自己是顾问角色，也不会越界指导你采取某种行动。当你说“你告诉我该怎么做”时，对方会回应：“我不知道啊，我没做过这份工作。还是回到你真正想做的事吧。”这种情况下反而有益处。当然，你不必非得有相关经验。（00:40:13）：所以我要说，教练的帮助非常强大。真希望自己能在职业生涯早期就接触到教练。答案或许是：教练比你想象的更触手可及。即便不是这样，我们所讨论的核心也在于——深入理解自身价值观、明确人生目标、激发内在好奇心——这些可以在任何年龄段被挖掘。无论你处于职业生涯的哪个阶段，都可以自问：什么对我最重要？（00:40:43）：我喜欢进行价值观探索，比如“你的价值观是什么？好吧，不。你的真正价值观是什么？” 这类问题你可以自己探索、质疑、学习。（00:40:53）：导师也很棒，尤其是那些不急于直接给出答案、而是通过提问、挑战你，提供思考空间的导师。（00:41:09）：优秀的管理者，尤其是顶尖的产品负责人，深知何时该戴上“教练帽”，何时该摘下“管理帽”，他们会明确说明：“好，我现在要摘下管理帽，戴上教练帽。伦尼，你真正想做什么？什么对你重要？你的职业生涯方向是什么？” 所以，我认为你可以从任何地方获得教练式的指导。（00:41:28）：你也可以进行自我指导。说实话，这就是我接受大量培训和指导后的收获之一——学会自我反思，比如当我感受到某种情绪时，会用教练式的问题自我剖析。这真的很强大。无论你是否有教练指导，都能做到这些。（00:41:46）：所以关键在于保持好奇心，深入了解真实的自己、珍视的东西，以及真正重要的事物。无论有没有教练的帮助，都能实现这些目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are there any resources that you love for either the values work or learning these questions to ask yourself? We can put them in the show notes if nothing comes to mind immediately. But is there something you recommend people check out?
turns.zh: 你们是否有特别推荐的资源，无论是关于价值观培养还是自我反思的学习内容？如果暂时想不到，我们可以把这些资源列入节目笔记。但如果你们有推荐的内容，欢迎分享。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah, there are some great books. Maybe I'll use this opportunity to throw out a couple suggestions.
turns.zh: 有啊，有几本很棒的书。或许我可以借此机会推荐几本。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 好啊。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: I guess we can link it into the show notes. Brene Brown's Dare to Lead. It's a good book. She actually even has a whole section in there around values, confronting her values. I like her approach. There's some free resources on her website. (00:42:26): I love Conscious Leadership Group's work here. The 15 Commitments of Conscious Leadership book is fantastic. You don't even need to buy the book. There's a ton of stuff on their website. Jim Dethmer, Diana Chapman and Kaley Warner Klemp are of the authors of that book. That's all about a lot of the stuff we've been talking about. They're the ones that have the above the line versus below the line that fits into this creative versus reactive standpoint. Those are all fantastic. (00:42:57): If you want to go deeper into more of the management science behind it, if you're like me and really curious about the psychology and the management science, Bob Anderson and Bill Adams's book, Mastering Leadership, creates the entire integrated system around creative versus reactive. (00:43:19): As a teaser, they identify five levels of leadership, of which reactive is the second, creative is the third. So beyond that, you get into integral and unitive. So if you're looking to unlock the advanced stages beyond creative, there's a lot of great stuff in there. Those are where all the research comes in as well. (00:43:38): From an adult development standpoint, Robert Kegan is the godfather of the adult-stage development work and the meaning-making that underlines a lot of this. He has a great book called Immunity to Change if you're curious about that.
turns.zh: 可以把链接放在节目笔记里啊。布琳·布朗的《敢于领导》这本书很不错。她在书中专门用一整章讨论价值观，以及如何直面自己的价值观。我很欣赏她的方法。她网站上还有一些免费资源。（00:42:26）：我很喜欢Conscious Leadership Group的工作。他们的《conscious Leadership的15项承诺》这本书非常棒。甚至不用买书，网站上就有大量资源。吉姆·德特默、戴安娜·查普曼和凯莉·华纳·克莱姆是这本书的作者。这些内容和我们讨论的很多观点不谋而合。他们提出的"表层领导"和"深层领导"的区分，与创意型和反应型领导的观点相契合，非常棒。（00:42:57）：如果想更深入了解背后的管理科学原理，如果你和我一样对心理学和管理科学感兴趣，鲍勃·安德森和比尔·亚当斯的《掌握领导力》一书构建了创意型与反应型领导的完整整合体系。（00:43:19）：作为一个预告，他们定义了五个领导力层次，其中反应型是第二层，创意型是第三层。更进一步的，还有整合型和统一型领导力。如果你想突破创意型领导的阶段，这里有很多精彩内容，也是相关研究的源泉。（00:43:38）：从成人发展视角看，罗伯特·凯根是成人发展阶段研究的权威，其意义建构理论是许多研究的基础。如果你对此感兴趣，他有一本很棒的书叫《免疫力》，值得一读。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. We will link to all those in the description of this podcast so folks don't have to Google around. I have a couple of more coaching questions before we move on to a few other topics. One is just what are you finding are the most common blind spots for product people in general? How are people shooting themselves in the foot most?
turns.zh: 太好了。我们会把所有这些资源链接到播客的节目说明里，这样大家就不用到处搜索了。在转入其他话题前，我还有几个关于教练的问题。首先，产品人员最常见的盲点是什么？大家最容易在哪些方面自毁长城？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Oh, that's a great question. I think probably the number one category, I'm not sure it's necessarily a problem, but maybe category or problems, is ... And this is, I think, great lesson for people earlier in their career, is how much all of the challenges that senior executives are dealing with come down to people versus product. So it's like it's fun to think about designing products, optimizing, doing user discovery, and testing what, but it's like you sit down with an executive and it's all about people. (00:44:47): That's the hard part. It's about persuading people, getting groups of people to want to work together, trying to figure out how to deal with difficult personalities, figuring out how to set a vision and articulate a vision, create an environment where people can collaborate and play. (00:45:01): And so, I think this category of blind spot often is people being confronted with that without having been intentional about thinking of it as a skill or an area that they needed to work on, needed to improve. (00:45:18): Part of what I think is pretty exciting about product management is you are a leader from day one in product management. There's leadership all over the place, but that's your job. You're a leader. You don't have any formal authority, but you're a leader. You're expected to lead. (00:45:39): Guess what? The hardest part about being a leader is when you don't get to just rely on the formal authority. So you're getting to practice all the hard parts about leadership from day one, because you're nobody's boss. You get to sharpen those skills, develop those intuitions, get better and better at that, so that when you do someday, if this is right for you, become someone else's boss, you've already been able to lean into that. (00:46:04): And so, the people side of this is such an incredible aspect of what product management is. What I find, and this may be a category of blind spots, is people realizing that when they're put in a position where they're expected to have impact and realizing that they haven't developed the skills, they haven't developed the capability to actually be able to manage and work through all these people, which is ...
turns.zh: 哦，这真是个好问题。我觉得最关键的一点——虽然我不确定这是否算个问题，但或许更应该称之为挑战或难题——就是……对于职业生涯早期的人来说，这是一个很好的教训，那就是高级管理者所面临的所有挑战，最终都归结于人际关系而非产品本身。比如，设计产品、优化流程、进行用户调研和测试这些工作固然有趣，但当你与高管们坐下来讨论时，所有话题都围绕着人际关系展开。（00:44:47）这才是难点所在。关键在于如何说服他人，如何让团队成员愿意协作，如何应对难相处的个性，如何设定并传达愿景，如何营造让人们能够协作和发挥的环境。（00:45:01）所以，我认为这种盲点往往出现在人们面对挑战时，却没有刻意将其视为需要提升的技能或领域。（00:45:18）我认为产品管理最令人兴奋的部分之一，是你从第一天起就是产品管理领域的领导者。到处都有领导力，但这就是你的职责所在。你是一名领导者，虽然没有正式权威，但你必须发挥领导作用。（00:45:39）猜猜看？作为领导者，最困难的部分就是无法依赖正式权威。因此，从第一天起你就需要磨练领导力的各个方面，因为你不是别人的上司。你要不断提升这些技能，培养这些直觉，精进到足以在未来——如果条件允许——成为别人的上司时，你早已胜任此职。（00:46:04）所以，人际交往方面是产品管理中最令人惊叹的方面。我发现（这或许也是一个盲点），当人们被赋予需要产生影响力的角色时，却意识到自己尚未掌握有效管理团队、解决人际问题的技能，这实在……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you actually get better at that or develop those skills?
turns.zh: 那要如何真正提升这方面的能力或培养这些技能呢？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah. I just think recognizing it is part of the job. It's important. Maybe I came up at a certain time where it was often dismissed as soft skills. It's just like soft skills are helpful, but they're not actually something you want to work on. They're not something you train, not something you ... (00:46:54): And this is just as important. This is the equal ... I wrote a piece recently about the art versus the science. The art is communication, collaboration, the more fuzzy, softer skills, people stuff. It's an elevation of that being just as important, if not more important, over time, as all this skills, techniques, tactics, managing a backlog, all that kind of stuff that you have to do. You should invest in that the same way you invest in those other skills. (00:47:25): So if you go off to a training to learn a technique for doing, I don't know, some sort of technical dashboard analysis, why don't you go to training to learn how to have difficult conversations? Because there's some great training about having difficult conversations, or do some training about storytelling. These are all really, really important factors that start to come into play. (00:47:54): What I would recommend is just appreciating that these are going to really, really matter and practicing and then valuing them and not thinking of them as something that either will matter later or a distraction or not really part of the job.
turns.zh: 是啊。我只是觉得认识到这一点是工作的一部分。这很重要。可能我成长的那个时代，人们常把这些视为软技能。软技能确实有用，但人们往往不愿去刻意培养它们。它们不是你能刻意训练的东西……（00:46:54）而这同样重要。这是平等的……我最近写了一篇关于艺术与科学的文章。艺术就是沟通、协作，更多的是模糊、软性的技能，人际交往方面的东西。随着时间推移，这些能力的重要性不亚于甚至超过所有那些技能、技巧、战术、管理积压任务之类的事情。你应该像投资其他技能一样去投资这些能力。（00:47:25）所以，如果你去参加培训学习某种技术分析，比如某种技术仪表盘分析，为什么不去参加学习如何进行困难对话的培训呢？因为有很棒的培训教你如何进行困难对话，或者参加一些讲故事的培训。这些都是非常、非常重要的因素，它们开始发挥作用了。（00:47:54）我建议大家要意识到这些能力真的非常重要，要去练习，然后重视它们，而不是把它们看作是以后才重要的东西，或者是分心之物，或者不是工作的一部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think the reason people don't do that work is because it's so hard. Difficult conversations are difficult. We talked about this with Trey Hass. But just like it's a rule of thumb, the thing that is hard is probably the thing you should be doing. It's like a compass point of you to the thing you should do.
turns.zh: 我觉得人们不做这些工作的原因是太难了。困难对话确实很难。我们和特雷·哈斯讨论过这个问题。但就像一条经验法则，难的事情往往就是你应该做的。这就像指引你前进的指南针。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Absolutely. We are all about doing hard stuff, product managers. That's what we're all about. And so, when something seems hard and it seems squishy and it seems like it's difficult to put a three-step rule around, chances are it's really going to matter. It goes back to this mindset shift. That means that there's an opportunity for you to readjust your inner complexity management system to adapt to that area of complexity that you're now seeing, because this stuff really feels squishy. And so, that's even more of a reason why you want to get your hands around it and grab onto it and value it and learn and grow from it.
turns.zh: 绝对的。我们产品经理就是要做困难的事情。这就是我们的职责所在。所以，当某件事看起来很难、模糊、难以用三步法则来概括时，很有可能它真的很重要。这又回到了思维模式的转变。这意味着你有机会重新调整你的内部复杂性管理系统，以适应你现在看到的复杂性领域，因为这些事情确实感觉模糊。所以，这更是一个你想要掌握它、抓住它、重视它、从中学习和成长的理由。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of difficult and squishy, I'm guessing that one of the biggest challenges that people you work with face and one of the most recurring themes is imposter syndrome, people having imposter syndrome, something definitely I went through and it comes up a lot on this podcast. What do you usually advise your clients to do when they're feeling imposter syndrome?
turns.zh: 说到困难和模糊，我猜你团队中的人面临的最大挑战之一，也是最常出现的主题之一，就是冒名顶替综合症，人们有这种感觉。我自己也经历过，在这个播客中也经常提到。当你的客户感到冒名顶替综合症时，你通常会建议他们怎么做？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah, it's a great question. I always get corrected to say imposter phenomenon by people in the psychology community, because I guess it's not a dysfunction. And so, I've learned to use their terms. But, yeah, I think just about everyone experiences it at some point. Research shows that that definitely is born out ... It's really the moments when you're doubting your abilities or you feel like a fraud or you feel like you don't belong. (00:49:54): It's funny because as I'm interrogating my own inner emotional state right now, I'm feeling it a little bit, because there's a part of me right now that's just like, "You're not a trained psychologist." When I said that whole thing, well, it's technically a phenomenon, there's a voice that was like, "What are you talking about? You don't know what you're talking about. Who are you [inaudible 00:50:14] on this?"
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实是个很棒的问题。心理学界的人总是纠正我，让我用“冒名顶替综合症”这个术语，因为他们认为这不算一种心理障碍。所以我也学会了用他们的术语。不过，我觉得几乎每个人都曾在某个时刻经历过这种感觉。研究表明，这种现象确实存在……它通常出现在你怀疑自己的能力、觉得自己是个骗子，或者觉得自己格格不入的时候。（00:49:54）：说来有趣，此刻我正在审视自己的内心情绪状态时，就隐约感觉到这种情绪了。因为现在我脑海里有个声音在说：“你又不是专业心理学家。”当我讲那些内容时，技术上讲这确实是一种心理现象，但有个声音却在质疑：“你在说什么呢？你根本不懂你在说什么。你算哪根葱？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We'll put a disclaimer on the episode.
turns.zh: 我们会在本期节目中添加免责声明。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah, I'm not a psychologist. So, look, we all feel it. There's a part of me right now that's like I'm going to say the wrong thing and embarrass myself. Product managers, product leaders maybe more so because the role is so cross-functional and ill-defined. There's always going to be an edge of the job that you aren't as qualified as whoever you're interacting with. It's the nature of it. Look, we're never going to be as good as an engineer, as good as a designer, as good ... So there's all these opportunities for that. (00:50:40): I find, certainly from client work, that there is a little bit of a softening and solidarity just knowing that. I'm just like, "Oh, you have that, too? Oh, I have that. Yeah, there's some value to that." (00:50:51): I think it's important to pause here and say that there is the risk of dismissing or even maybe weaponizing imposter phenomenon against particular populations, particularly women, people of color of all genders, women of color especially, who are facing real external feedback and doubt about their abilities. (00:51:15): The environment is reinforcing and the source of a lot of this stuff, microaggressions, bias, real aggressions. And so, I think we always have to be careful in the helping professions to not dismiss it as a problem that just shifts the obligation to the person. So it's like, "Oh, that's just your imposter syndrome. Deal with it." Well, it's really easy to overlook all these systemic issues that are leading to that imposter syndrome. (00:51:39): So the leaders I work with, I think we have a special obligation both to confront our own inner dynamic, but also to recognize what our role is in the broader environment that might be contributing to some of this stuff. If you're a leader, you have a special obligation to dismantle those, not when you're meeting with your people, be like, "Ah, it's just your imposter syndrome. You can work through it. Hire a coach," but to be able to recognize, "Okay, wait, what signals are you getting? What issues are contributing to this? What's our role in needing to change that?" So I think that's worth pointing out. (00:52:13): By the way, there's a great article in Harvard Business Review from a couple of years ago. I think the title was literally Stop Telling Women They Have Imposter Syndrome. The two authors of that were Ruchika Tulshyan and Jodi-Ann Burey, if you're curious and you want to go into more depth on that. (00:52:29): As coaches there, there's all sorts of ways we're trained to work with this. Oftentimes as an inner critic and inner voice, we all have voices, saboteurs. They're often trying to help us, they have good intentions, but they're developed to try to protect us in certain ways. So gaining awareness of those, just sort of like, "Oh, that is an inner critic. That's what it's trying to do." There's a self-distancing that's valuable to that, really kind of ... (00:52:54): I like to think of it a little bit as you got inner border directors, and there's some noisy, chatty voices that every so often sit in the chairperson's seat and start taking over. If you start to recognize, "Wait, no, I'm the chairperson. I don't want to hear from you right now. We'll hear from you later," it starts to create some power and you start to notice when it's happening. (00:53:16): We bypass inner critic sometimes as a classic coaching technique. It's like, "Okay, I'm sounding that's your inner critic is saying that. What if we just ask it to maybe step aside? Let's keep talking here." (00:53:28): You can befriend it. There's a lot of practices and works just actually trying to understand what its motivations are. You can think of it as a board. Give this board member a new job, put it on a new committee, reassign it. (00:53:41): There's oftentimes underlying belief systems. We talked before about my impression of what a real leader was and who they had to be. And so, hey, when all those second-guessing of me not being a real leader, of me not being qualified came from some of those underlying assumptions, that that was the only type of leader that was effective, was somebody that was slamming their fist out on the table. (00:54:02): Okay, so what if we redefine that? I'm too kind to be a leader. I'm not dominating, commanding enough. When you hear a client say that as a coach, you recognize, okay, there's a connection being made here between what effective leadership is and isn't. Let's interrogate that connection. Is that connection actually true? (00:54:21): Again, it get backs to this question of you're often responding to other styles, approaches you've seen. You're comparing yourself to others. So this is the reactive mindset of I'm always comparing myself to that person, to that wave, that being, and seeing myself as lesser then. And so, the inner work of starting to see who I really am truly inside and less comparing myself to others. (00:54:42): But, yeah, imposter phenomenon, syndrome, whatever you want to call it, very common and very popular, I suppose. Although when I say popular, it's like popular like a play.
turns.zh:
是的，我不是心理学家。所以，你看，我们都能感同身受。现在我内心有个声音，总觉得自己会说错话，出丑。产品经理和产品负责人尤其如此，因为这个角色跨职能性强且定义模糊。总有一些工作领域，你会觉得自己不如合作伙伴。这种职业特性摆在那里。听着，我们永远比不上工程师，比不上设计师……所以总有各种机会让你意识到这一点。（00:50:40）：从客户项目中我发现，只要大家知道这一点，就能稍微缓解压力，增强团结感。我会想：“哦，你也有这种感受？哦，我也有。是啊，这还是有价值的。” （00:50:51）：这里需要暂停一下，指出有一种危险——我们可能会轻易否定或利用冒名顶替综合症来针对特定群体，尤其是女性、有色人种，以及女性有色人种群体。她们面临着真实的外部反馈和对自身能力的质疑。（00:51:15）：环境本身就是放大这种现象的温床，微歧视、偏见、直接攻击层出不穷。因此，我们在帮助他人时，必须谨慎，避免将问题归咎于个人，然后说“哦，这只是你的冒名顶替综合症。自己克服吧。”但这样做很容易忽视导致这种综合症的系统性问题。（00:51:39）：我与之共事的领导者们，认为我们有特殊责任既要面对自身的内心动态，也要认识到我们在更广泛环境中可能导致这些问题的角色。如果你是领导者，你有特殊义务拆解这些问题：不要在开会时说“哦，这只是你的冒名顶替综合症。自己克服吧。请个教练吧。”而是能够意识到：“好的，等等，你接收到什么信号了？哪些问题导致了这些问题？我们在改变现状中扮演着怎样的角色？” 所以我觉得这一点值得强调。（00:52:13）：顺便说一句，几年前《哈佛商业评论》上有一篇很棒的文章。文章标题直译为《别再告诉女性她们有冒名顶替综合症了》。作者是鲁奇卡·图尔什扬和乔迪-安·布雷，如果你感兴趣想深入了解，可以去看看。（00:52:29）：作为教练，我们接受过各种应对这种情况的训练。通常会把它们视为内在批评者和内在声音。我们都有这样的声音，自我破坏者。他们往往出于好意，但发展出的模式是为了保护我们。所以要认识到这些声音，意识到“哦，这就是内在批评者。它想做的是……” 保持自我距离对此非常重要，真的……（00:52:54）：我喜欢把它比作内部边境官员，有一些吵闹、爱说话的声音，时不时会占据主席的位置并开始接管。如果你开始意识到：“等等，不，我才是主席。我现在不想听你说话。等会儿再说。”就能创造出一些力量，并且你会注意到这种情况何时发生。（00:53:16）：有时我们会绕过内在批评者，这是一种经典的教练技巧。比如，“好的，我听到内在批评者在说这些。不如我们请它退一步？我们继续聊吧。” （00:53:28）：你可以和它成为朋友。有很多实践方法……
实际上，我的工作就是试图理解他们的动机。你可以把这看作是一块棋盘。给这位董事会成员分配新工作，安排他加入新委员会，重新调配他的职责。（00:53:41）：很多时候存在着隐藏的信念体系。我们之前讨论过我对真正领导者的印象，以及他们应该具备怎样的特质。所以，当有人质疑我不是真正的领导者，不够胜任时，其实这些质疑源于一些潜在的假设——他们认为只有那种在会议上拍桌子、强势主导的领导风格才是有效的。（00:54:02）：好吧，那如果我们重新定义这种领导模式呢？我太善良了，不适合当领导。我不够强势、不够有威严。当你作为教练听到客户这样说时，你会意识到，客户在这里将有效领导和无效领导混为一谈。让我们来剖析这种关联。这种关联真的准确吗？（00:54:21）：这又回到了你经常模仿他人风格和方法的问题。你总是在拿自己和别人比较。这就是被动反应的心态——我总是在和那个人、那股潮流、那个存在比较，觉得自己不够优秀。所以，关键在于从内心深处认识真实的自己，减少与他人的比较。（00:54:42）：不过，嗯，冒名顶替综合症、自卑情结之类的，我想这种现象很常见也很受关注。虽然我说"受关注"，可能更像是一种流行文化现象。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. Another inner critic tactic I've heard that I used for a bit that was helpful is to give your inner critic a name, like Jim. I mean like, "Jim, not right now. I don't need you right now." That kind of helps.
turns.zh: 好的。我听说过另一种应对内心批评者的技巧，我曾尝试过一段时间，效果不错——给你的内心批评者起个名字，比如叫吉姆。比如说：“吉姆，现在别插嘴，我现在不需要你。”这样能起到一定帮助作用。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah. There is a whole school of coaching that I've worked with that's called parts work or internal family systems. It comes from a psychologist named Richard Schwartz who determined this. It can be really, really powerful. (00:55:19): I'll word my clients and we will give them names. We will imagine what they look like. They will interview these parts. If you've seen the Pixar movie Inside Out, this notion that like, hey, all these different parts show up in different ways. I'm going to put myself, the real me, the real self into the chairperson's seat. When I hear these voices, I'm going to appreciate them from what they are and who they are. They're not me. They're parts of me. (00:55:46): There's something really powerful in that, in that sense of like ... Because, otherwise, they're all me. So I just hear this voice telling me I'm an idiot and I'm a clown and I'm not qualified to be in this room. Then when you can start to go, "Oh, yeah, there it is. That's Larry Loser. My big angry, irritating judge who's, of course ... Oh, yeah, Larry always shows up every time I do something new, because Larry doesn't want me to challenge myself. So, of course, Larry's going to pipe in. I've heard from Larry. I'm going to ask Larry to step aside. Let's go." Yeah, it can be very powerful.
turns.zh: 是的。有一整个心理学流派叫“部件疗法”或“内在家庭系统疗法”，我曾参与相关实践。这源于心理学家理查德·施瓦茨的研究成果，效果非常显著。（00:55:19）我会和客户一起给他们的内心批评者起名字，构想他们的外形特征，并让这些批评者参与对话。如果你看过皮克斯电影《头脑特工队》，就会明白不同批评者的表现各异。我会把真实的自己置于“主席”的位置，当听到这些批评声音时，要接纳它们本来的面目和存在意义——它们不是我，而是我内在的不同部分。（00:55:46）这种方法的强大之处在于……因为否则，它们全都等同于“我”。比如，当听到“你是个白痴、跳梁小丑，根本不配坐在这间会议室里”这样的声音时，要能分辨出：“哦，对，就是拉里·失败者。他那个暴躁易怒、爱评判我的家伙，当然……每次我尝试新事物时，拉里总会跳出来阻止我。所以，他现在又来捣乱了。我早就料到了。我要请拉里退场，继续前进。”这种方法确实很有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. One last question about coaching. For folks that want to find a coach, do you have any advice of just how to find a coach, and then what are a couple questions you can ask to evaluate if they're a good fit for you?
turns.zh: 太棒了。最后一个关于心理咨询的问题。对于想找心理咨询师的人，你有什么建议吗？比如如何找到合适的咨询师，以及可以问哪些问题来评估是否匹配？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah, great question. So I think, like any helping profession, finding a therapist or really anyone who you're going to have a deep and lasting relationship with, this sort of trust and authenticity is really important. I think we all, as coaches, recognize, and we feel this as well with clients, is it either has to be a fit or not. Sometimes it's hard to put your finger on it. Sometimes you meet with someone and you're like, "Yeah, it clicks. It feels right." Sometimes you're like, "Eh, it doesn't," and that's okay. And so, all coaches worth their salt will offer a free session to understand that, engage that. (00:57:13): I always tell everyone in that session, if you don't decide to work with me or I decide ... We don't need a reason. It's fine. It's just not a fit, and that's okay. You don't need to come up with bullet point reasons to let me down. It's part of how it goes. (00:57:28): You might prefer certain people, certain gender, certain backgrounds. You may feel more comfortable or less comfortable with ... Maybe you want an old guy like me. Maybe you want an old guy like me, and that's fine. It has to feel right. (00:57:41): I would ask them to talk to you about what coaching is to them, because, again, it might combine some of these more mentory things. It might be more tactical. Some coaches are more structured, "Week one, we're going to do this. Week two, we're going to do this. Week ... " Others are more pure coaches like me, where, look, within the first five minutes, I'm going to ask you what you want to talk about today, because you're bringing the agenda. So figure that out. Figure out what works for you. (00:58:07): Then I think there's a lot of great places to go. Actually, specifically where to go, the International Coaching Federation is our governing body. So those of us that are credentialed coaches you'll find there. Again, you don't have to be credentialed, but that'll be a great place to find people who are. (00:58:23): There are some matchmaking services, BetterUp, Torch, or some of the more accessible ones. There's one called Prismaticco. It's a little bit more higher end for more senior execs. Scale just put out a list of top coaches who work with product managers and product leaders, all sorts of great coaches. We can include that link. Lenny, I think you're involved.
turns.zh: 是的，这个问题问得好。所以我认为，就像任何助人行业一样，要找到一位治疗师，或者任何你能与之建立深厚持久关系的人，这种信任和真诚感都非常重要。我想我们作为教练，都能意识到——而且与客户一起时也能感受到——这种关系要么合适，要么不合适。有时很难用言语来形容。有时你与某人见面后，会觉得“嗯，感觉很对劲，挺合适的”。有时则会觉得“哎呀，不合适”，没关系的。所以，所有称职的教练都会提供免费咨询环节来了解这种情况，并进行互动。（00:57:13）：在那次咨询中，我总是告诉大家，如果你决定不与我合作，或者我决定不与你合作……无需给出理由。这没关系。就是不合适，就这样。没必要找些冠冕堂皇的理由来敷衍我。这就是这个行业的常态。（00:57:28）：你可能会偏爱某些人、某些性别、某些背景。你可能会觉得与某些人相处更自在，或者更不自在……也许你希望找个像我这样的老家伙。没关系的。关键是感觉要对。（00:57:41）：我会让他们谈谈教练对他们的意义，因为，正如我所说，可能融合了更多指导性的元素。也可能更偏向战术层面。有些教练结构化得很强，“第一周我们做这个，第二周做那个……”。而像我这样的纯粹型教练，在前五分钟就会问你今天想聊什么，因为议程是你们自己定的。所以要根据自己的需求来选择。（00:58:07）：我觉得有很多不错的平台可以参考。具体来说，国际教练联合会是我们的行业监管机构。在那里能找到获得认证的教练。当然，不一定要认证，但那里能找到很多认证教练。（00:58:23）：还有一些配对服务，比如BetterUp、Torch之类的，或者更易用的平台。还有一个叫Prismaticco的，针对资深高管的更高端平台。Scale刚刚发布了一份与产品经理和产品负责人合作的顶级教练名单，里面有很多优秀的教练。我们可以附上链接。Lenny，我记得你也参与其中了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Congrats on winning one of their categories for best coach of ... Which category was that?
turns.zh: 是啊。你获奖了，荣获最佳教练奖项之一……是哪个奖项来着？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Product leaders. So, yeah, this was just a setup for you to say that. But thank you. But there's tons of great coach, and different styles, different stages of careers. I think all those folks have work with or have worked with product folks. (00:59:03): And so, again, just talk to a few. Reach out to a few. Ask them. If you're looking for more names, ask people who you admire, whose leadership styles you like and want to emulate, who they recommend, because oftentimes they have a better understanding of, hey, this is the type of coach that may want to work with, more of the emotional work, or this is the type of coach who actually maybe has a more compatible vision of what you're looking for, because, look, all coaches are different. You can tell I'm a touchy-feely heart coach. (00:59:35): There are coaches who are ... Sometimes people want a coach and they're just like, "You grab that brass ring. We're going to pound the table. I'm going to push you. I'm going to challenge you. I'm going to beat you up. I'm going to be more of a drill sergeant." That's a different style of coach that works with other people. That may be more what you're looking for. (00:59:50): So I would just talk to a bunch, do some free sessions, get an opportunity to explore it. I coach people in the free session. So it's not just like we're talking. We're going to talk about something. I'm going to coach you. You're going to get a sense of what this looks like. Then come away and just ask yourself, what are your goals and where was there a fit? If there's not, just keep looking.
turns.zh: 产品领袖。好吧，这么说其实是为你铺垫的，不过还是谢谢你。不过优秀的教练实在太多了，他们风格各异，处于职业生涯的不同阶段。我觉得这些人都曾与产品团队合作过，或者正在合作中。（00:59:03）：所以，再次强调，多和几位聊聊，主动联系几位。去问问他们。如果你想获取更多推荐名单，可以向你敬仰的人士请教——那些你欣赏其领导风格、渴望效仿的人——让他们推荐，因为他们往往更清楚哪些教练适合你，或许更能理解你的情感诉求，或许能与你的愿景更契合，毕竟每个教练都各不相同。我明显是个情感导向型的心理教练。（00:59:35）：有些教练……有时候人们找教练时会说：“你要勇攀高峰。我们要拍桌子。我要鞭策你。我要挑战你。我要严格要求你。”这种风格的教练适合其他人。或许这才是你真正需要的。（00:59:50）：所以多和几位聊聊，参加几次免费咨询，借此机会探索一下。我在免费咨询中会指导学员。不会只是聊天，而是会围绕某个主题展开。我会指导你，让你了解这种指导方式是怎样的。然后离开时，你就能问问自己：我的目标是什么？我们是否契合？如果不契合，那就继续寻找。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. That was very tactically helpful. I really appreciate all those resources. We'll definitely link to all that in the description. I have just a couple questions I wanted to ask you outside of coaching, around some of your posts that you've written before we get to our exciting lightning round. One is around this idea of 10X versus 10%. (01:00:26): So you wrote this post about the importance of thinking 10X versus 10%. Truthfully, I actually had a post started, "10X versus 10%." I was like, "Oh, this is going to be great." Then I Googled, "Oh, Ken's already written about it." So I'm glad that you have written about it and written about it so well.
turns.zh: 太棒了。这真是实用的建议。我非常感谢这些资源。我们肯定会在描述中附上所有链接。在进入精彩的闪电问答环节之前，我想问几个与教练领域无关的问题，关于你之前写的一些帖子。第一个是关于10倍增长与10%改进的概念。（01:00:26）：你写过一篇关于思考10倍增长而非10%改进的重要性的文章。说实话，我也曾起草过一篇题为《10倍增长与10%改进》的文章。当时我特别兴奋，结果一搜发现肯已经写过了。所以很高兴你能写出如此精彩的文章。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Great minds think alike, as they say.
turns.zh: 正所谓英雄所见略同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Now I don't have to write it. I'd love to just hear your general take on what this idea is and how to think about 10X or 10% bets.
turns.zh: 现在我不必自己写了。我很想听听你对这个概念的总体看法，以及如何思考10倍增长或10%改进的赌注。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Again, I'm a great synthesizer of ideas. This isn't my idea. This is a lot of ... It came from some thinking at Google and some push. I think it's really the sense that we think too small sometimes. You'll see that as a theme for some of the other things I've written too. There needs to be a push. If you really want to have huge breakthrough innovation, you need to be able to try, you need to be able to fail. You need to be able to shoot for the moon is where this 10X comes from. (01:01:22): A lot of it is mindset, but a lot of it is also cultural. It's creating environments where ... And I had the great privilege of working at Google for 14 years. I felt like it was definitely an environment that I got to play in, of being willing to take big swings that might fail. (01:01:36): This doesn't mean that the company could all be out of business tomorrow. But it's like if you have a choice between trying something that could have a massive breakthrough, a massive change, and playing small ball where you're going to get a bunch of 10% improvements, you are over time, if you're willing to try, if you're willing to fail, if you're willing to push yourself, if you're willing to think bigger, if you're willing to create environments, great ideas come from places that are unexpected, you'll achieve massive, massive breakthrough. (01:02:02): You can find the piece on my website, because I use examples from history, but it is a little bit of being brave and trying big things. If you look at all the great technology, the huge breakthrough innovations that we've had, the coronavirus vaccine, just this ... Man, there is no small balling that. That was a big, big swing that there was no guarantee of success, but we were willing to try it. We were willing to fail knowing that failure was probably the more likely outcome in the chance that we would achieve something that would really have that level of breakthrough. (01:02:36): And so, I think it is what I always challenge leaders to do is create the environment where people can step in and bring those types of ideas, and not play it safe or not be like, "Ah, boy, that seems like a big one. If we bring that to the CEO, there's no way they'll take a chance. So let's ramp down our expectations. Let's bring this little idea in that is a little bit more guaranteed to work." (01:03:01): And so, it is the obligation of leaders to create that environment for people to be able to innovate, because the ideas are out there. I use the example of Kodak. Kodak invented the digital camera. It wasn't like, oh, people at Kodak were dumb. They didn't know digital was coming. No, they literally invented the digital camera. There just wasn't an environment created where the people who had that idea, who saw that potential, who saw that possibility could step up through the plate and try.
turns.zh: 再次强调，我善于整合各种想法。这不是我的独创理念。这源于谷歌内部的一些思考和推动。我认为问题往往在于我们有时想得太局限了。你会发现，我写的其他一些文章也都围绕这个主题。需要有推动力。若想实现重大突破性创新，就必须敢于尝试、敢于失败。勇于追求远大目标，这正是“10倍效应”的来源。（01:01:22）：这很大程度上关乎思维模式，但也与企业文化息息相关。关键在于营造这样的环境……我有幸在谷歌工作了14年。我深切感受到，那里确实是一个允许人们大胆尝试、敢于冒险的土壤。（01:01:36）：这并不意味着公司明天就会倒闭。但当你面临两个选择：要么尝试可能带来巨大突破、引发剧烈变革的创新，要么选择保守策略、追求10%的微小改进时，假以时日，只要你愿意尝试、愿意承受失败、愿意突破自我、愿意放大格局，伟大的创意总会从意想不到的地方涌现，你就能实现突破性创新。（01:02:02）：你可以在我的网站上找到相关内容，因为我引用了历史案例，但核心在于勇于尝试大事。回顾所有伟大的科技成果、突破性创新，比如新冠疫苗，哪个不是大胆尝试？没有人能保证成功，但我们愿意冒险。正是这种无所畏惧的精神，让我们实现了突破。（01:02:36）：所以，我始终呼吁领导者创造这样的环境，让人们能大胆提出这些想法，不要墨守成规，不要想：“天哪，这主意太大了。如果拿给CEO，他肯定不会冒险。还是降低预期，把这个更易成功的小想法提出来吧。” （01:03:01）：因此，领导者有责任为创新创造环境，因为创意本身就存在。我举个例子，柯达公司发明了数码相机。并非因为柯达员工愚钝、没预见数码时代的到来，而是他们实实在在地发明了数码相机。只是当时的环境不允许有远见卓识的人大胆尝试。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have any rules of thumb of how many of your ideas/resources should go into these big ideas versus incremental 10% bets, or is the general advice just like people aren't thinking big enough, often enough, so you should always think a little bit bigger than you naturally will?
turns.zh: 对于这些大创意和10%的渐进式改进，您是否有经验法则，建议投入多少资源？还是说一般建议是人们往往想得不够大胆、不够频繁，所以应该比自然倾向更大胆地思考？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: I think it depends. I mean it depends on the company. If you work in R&D, in labs, maybe everything is in that category and you build a portfolio. If you're a venture capital seed investor, or if you're working at a research lab, it's like you're building a huge portfolio of these bets. You're just assuming that maybe 99 of them will fail, but one will succeed and it'll make it all worthwhile. (01:04:09): Most of us aren't in those environments. We're in places where we have real customers buying our products, wanting our products, using our products. We're like, "Let's bet the entire company own 50 things that may not work out." It may not be right for you. (01:04:20): So I think it is a little bit of an approach. I think it needs to be thought of in a fractal way, though, because maybe at the company level, they're thinking Google once upon a time had a 70-20-10 thing, whereas 70% is our core business. It's the time we're searching ads. 20% is adjacent business, and then 10% on crazy bets that may not be anything. (01:04:43): But I think that's at the company level. At the individual level, at your team level, you might have your own way of thinking. You're just like, okay, I've got 12 engineers on the team. We're working on, at any time, a bunch of stuff that we know we have to do. This is a bunch of stuff that we hope is like 10%. Then we're going to create some space for some innovation. Maybe it's just one engineer every sprint, or it's like a couple of times a year. (01:05:09): You create that type of space in your own little air bubble that isn't necessarily at the portfolio level, to try things that may not work. But if they do, the payoff will be so substantial that it'll make the whole thing worthwhile.
turns.zh:
我觉得这得看情况。我是说，这取决于所在的公司。如果你从事研发工作，比如在实验室工作，也许所有工作都属于这一类，你需要建立一个项目组合。如果你是一名风险投资种子投资人，或者在研究实验室工作，那就相当于你在进行大量押注。你只是假设其中99个项目可能会失败，但只要有一个成功，就能让一切都值了。（01:04:09）：我们大多数人并不处于那种环境。我们身处的环境是，客户购买我们的产品、需要我们的产品、使用我们的产品。我们会想：“让我们押上整个公司的赌注，尝试50个可能失败的项目。” 但这可能不适合你。
（01:04:20）：所以我认为这是一种方法。不过，需要用分形思维来考虑，因为在公司层面，他们可能曾推行过70-20-10的策略，即70%是核心业务，20%是相关业务，10%是可能失败的疯狂赌注。
（01:04:43）：但这是在公司层面。在个人层面、团队层面，你可能有自己的思考方式。比如，团队有12名工程师，我们随时都在做一堆必须完成的工作。这些工作占据了团队80%的时间，然后我们会为创新腾出空间。也许每个冲刺周期就让一名工程师负责创新，或者每年只进行几次创新。
（01:05:09）：你可以在自己的小圈子里创造这种创新空间，不一定非要在项目组合层面进行尝试。但如果成功了，回报将非常丰厚，一切努力都将值得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Very helpful. Next question is around I think your most popular post that you've ever written, and maybe the thing that put you on the radar of writing, is around how to hire a product manager. Maybe this is where you mentioned donuts the first time. Is that right, or no?
turns.zh: 太棒了。非常有帮助。下一个问题是关于你写过的最受欢迎的文章，或许也是让你受到关注的文章，那就是如何招聘产品经理。也许你第一次提到“甜甜圈”就是在这篇文章里。对吗？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: It's funny. I think that was later.
turns.zh: 很有趣。我记得那是后来提到的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah, I think that was a talk that came after that.
turns.zh: 是的，那是那之后的一次演讲。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool.
turns.zh: 好的，不错。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah, that was definitely the big one for me.
turns.zh: 是的，那对我来说确实很重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So here's the question, just to keep it simple, what's one piece of advice that you would give people trying to hire a product manager? What's the thing that you think is most maybe missed or useful?
turns.zh: 所以问题是，简单来说，对于试图招聘产品经理的人，你会给出什么建议？你认为最容易被忽视或最有用的点是什么？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah, I think the intangibles. So basically I wrote that originally as an email, that it was a copy pasta thing for me, where people kept coming to me and being like, "Hey, I think we're going to try to hire a product manager or a company. Can you send over a sample job description?" I'd be like, "Yeah. Before we write the job description, let's talk about what the job is, because I'm not sure we all mean the same thing." And so, then I wrote that ... It was in 2005, so this goes back ... to try to define what the role actually is. (01:06:31): I actually feel like maybe the pendulum shifted way too far now where it's the interview process is so structured. Everyone's doing all these mock. They know exactly what questions they're going to get. It's SAT prep. Everyone's ready. But we've missed out with can they do the job? Because it's like they can pass the interview, but can they do the job? (01:06:53): And so, I think you have to be careful. This is particularly the case if you are a smaller company. You don't have a huge apparatus of Google and Meta, where you've got interviewing monolith of getting persuaded into ... Maybe this goes back a little bit to the science and the art. They passed all the technical questions. They do all this, they do all that. They do all that. But then you neglect to find out can this person show up and work with these engineers, these designers? Can they inspire them? Is this somebody that they want to follow? Do they have the right mindset for what this job entails? Do we even have an agreement on what their job is going to be? (01:07:35): The number of people you see earlier in their career will be like, "Well, I thought I was hiring for this, but it turns that's not even product management," or it was like, "I thought I was going to do this, but all they want me to do is build fee." It's like how'd that not come out in the group process? It's like, well, I know how it didn't come out because they answered a whole bunch of structured questions around ... They did a programming exercise and they did a presentation and nobody stopped to ask. (01:07:55): And so, I think that's really the big thing from an interviewer perspective. I think same thing goes for the candidate's perspective. You are interviewing a potential employer. You're interviewing a boss. You're interviewing coworkers. What do you want? What do you care about? What is the type of place you want to be in? What do you not want to be in? How are you evaluating that? How are you asking those questions? (01:08:18): Yeah, salary matters, title. All that kind of stuff matters. But you're interviewing a place to plop yourself into. How are you approaching that to make sure you're making the right decision?
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得关键在于那些无形的因素。基本上，我最初写那篇邮件时，那只是个模板化的回复。当时总有人来找我，说：“嘿，我们打算招聘产品经理或者组建团队。你能发一份样本职位描述吗？”我就会回答：“好啊。在写职位描述之前，先聊聊这个职位到底是什么吧，因为我不确定大家理解的是否一致。” 然后，我写了那份邮件……那是在2005年，现在回想起来……就是想明确这个角色的职责到底是什么。（01:06:31）：我现在觉得，可能面试流程的标准化已经走得太极端了。大家都在进行模拟面试，知道自己会被问到哪些问题。就像SAT备考一样，所有人都准备充分。但我们忽略了最重要的问题：他们能胜任这份工作吗？他们能通过面试，但能实际胜任工作吗？（01:06:53）：所以，面试官要格外谨慎。特别是对于小公司来说尤其如此。没有谷歌和Meta那样庞大的招聘机器，无法通过结构化面试来筛选候选人。但我们却忽略了关键问题：他们能否与工程师和设计师团队合作？能否激励他们？是否值得追随？他们是否具备胜任这份工作的思维模式？我们是否对职位职责达成了共识？（01:07:35）：我见过很多初入职场的人会说：“我以为招聘的是这个职位，但结果发现根本不是产品经理。”或者“我以为自己要做这个，但他们只让我写代码。”这些问题在面试过程中为何没有被发现？其实我知道原因，因为他们回答了大量结构化问题，做了编程题和演示，却没人停下来追问。（01:07:55）：所以，从面试官的角度来看，这才是关键。候选人同样需要审视：你面试的是潜在雇主、上司和同事。你想得到什么？你关心什么？你希望在怎样的环境中工作？你不愿接受什么？你如何评估这些？如何提出这些问题？（01:08:18）：薪资和职位头衔固然重要，但你要融入这个团队。如何确保自己做出了正确的选择？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round, where I'm going to ask you a few questions and whatever comes to mind, just give me an answer. That's it. Very simple. Does that sound good?
turns.zh: 好的，接下来是我们激动人心的闪电问答环节。我会问你们几个问题，想到什么就回答什么。就这么简单。听起来不错吧？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah. Inner critic is raging right now.
turns.zh: 好的。内心的自我批评现在正在肆虐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, no. Real-time imposter syndrome.
turns.zh: 哦，不。实时冒名顶替综合症。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Here we go.
turns.zh: 开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 01:08:49].

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So question one, what are two or three books that you recommend most to other people?
turns.zh: 好的。第一个问题，请推荐两到三本你最常向他人推荐的书籍？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Oh, 15 Commitments of Conscious Leadership. Definitely on that book. I'd just add books I've never recommended before. Probably Innovators Dilemma. It's probably my number one favorite book for product managers and product leaders.
turns.zh: 哦，《有意识领导力的15项承诺》。这本书我肯定会推荐的。我还想再加几本我从未推荐过的书。可能是《创新者的窘境》。这本书可能是产品经理和产品领导者最喜欢的书了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. What's a recent movie or TV show that you've liked?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你最近看过喜欢的电影或电视剧吗？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: I love Ms. Marvel. My whole family were really enjoying it. I love all the MCU stuff. We just eat it up. Ms. Marvel has been amazing. Then watching Barry, which is crazy. It's sort of like nothing else I think ever on TV. Then, over the last year, probably Severance. It's my favorite program over the last ... I'd say last year.
turns.zh: 我超爱《惊奇队长》。我们全家都特别喜欢看。我喜欢漫威宇宙的所有作品，简直爱不释手。《惊奇队长》太棒了。然后看《闪电侠》，这部剧简直太疯狂了。我觉得电视上没哪部剧能比得上它。过去一年，可能最喜欢的还是《断头谷》。这是我去年最喜欢的剧集。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Yeah. That is a trippy show. I've watched it all. We might be severed people, we don't even know.
turns.zh: 哇。是啊。这部剧太烧脑了。我全看完了。说不定我们就是被割裂的人呢，自己都不知道。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: You won't even know.
turns.zh: 你绝对猜不到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. What is a favorite interview question that you like to ask folks when you interview them?
turns.zh: 好的。你面试别人时最喜欢问的一个问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Well, actually let me flip it because I just talked about interviewing as the interview ... Maybe I'll ask a favorite question for people who are being interviewed to ask the employer. Is that fair or is that turn the tables too much?
turns.zh: 嗯，实际上我要反过来问，因为我刚说了面试时作为面试官……或许我该问被面试者最想问雇主的问题。这样公平吗？会不会太反客为主了？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. Yes.
turns.zh: 我喜欢。没错。

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: I think a great question ... Actually maybe I have a couple. I think one question that I love is how does the company define a product team? Because it answers so much. It says so much about culture, collaboration, decision-making, the role of product management. If there's one question and you could figure out what is this culture like, it would be asking that. (01:10:20): I think another great question for candidates is to ask them to pick an example of something they've shipped recently and just talk about how it came to be. How did the bill become a law? Was it somebody in sales yelled and it got added to the backlog and it was the next thing? Is it a group of people together understanding customer user needs through discovery and ideating and trying some things and testing it? It says a lot about what it would be like to work there, particularly when it comes to empowerment and product culture. So those are probably two good questions.
turns.zh: 我觉得一个很棒的问题……实际上我有几个。我最喜欢的一个问题是公司如何定义产品团队？因为这能透露很多信息。它能反映出文化、协作、决策机制，还有产品管理的角色。如果你能从这个问题中了解到公司的文化，那再好不过了。（01:10:20）：我觉得对候选人来说，另一个很棒的问题是让他们举例说明最近上线的产品是如何诞生的。是销售部门发脾气把需求加到待办列表里，然后就成了下一个项目？还是团队通过发现用户需求、构思创意、尝试验证等方式共同完成的？这能透露出很多关于公司工作环境的信息，特别是关于授权和产品文化方面。所以这两个问题应该都不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Those are really good questions. I'm going to steal them. Final question, who else in the industry do you respect as a thought leader? I imagine this list is very long, but what comes to mind?
turns.zh: 这些问题确实很棒。我要把它们记下来。最后一个问题，你在行业里最尊敬的思想领袖是谁？我猜这份名单很长，但你能想到谁？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Well, this list is all of my fellow podcast guests on your podcast, Lenny, which is, speaking of imposter phenomenon, is just an incredible group of all the folks that I love and admire. I think, though, because ... Maybe I'll answer it a little bit outside of product, because I would worry that I would leave out too many great names. (01:11:26): In the realms of leadership, Amy Edmondson is somebody I really admire. She's done a lot of the work on psychological safety. I really, really value her work, her contributions. There's a guy named Tom Garrity, who has a newsletter about psychological safety. I think he's collaborated with Amy before. It's one of the best, not the best newsletter I received, Lenny, maybe the second best, about psychological safety for those of us that are wanting to create environments where people can really thrive and do their best. (01:12:05): In the coaching profession, I mean the coaching profession emerges from the humanist psychology traditions or the client-first work of ... Carl Rogers and Abraham Maslow are intellectual heroes of mine. They're both dead. I don't know if we're supposed to talk about living people here, but definitely as I think about in my profession, they really set the stage and created the environment that coaching could even exist. So I'll include them.
turns.zh: 嗯，这份名单上都是你播客《Lenny》的嘉宾，说到冒名顶替综合症，他们都是我非常敬重和喜爱的一群人。不过我觉得，因为……也许我应该稍微避开产品领域来回答这个问题，因为我担心会遗漏太多优秀的人名。（01:11:26）：在领导力领域，艾米·埃德蒙森是我非常钦佩的人。她在心理安全方面做了很多研究。我真的非常重视她的工作和贡献。还有一个叫汤姆·加里蒂的人，他有一份关于心理安全的时事通讯。我记得他之前和艾米合作过。这是我收到的关于心理安全的最佳（不算最佳，但可能是第二佳）时事通讯之一，对于那些想创造让人们真正蓬勃发展、发挥最佳水平的环境的人来说，这份通讯堪称宝藏。（01:12:05）：在教练行业，我指的是源自人本主义心理学传统或以客户为先的工作理念……卡尔·罗杰斯和亚伯拉罕·马斯洛都是我的精神偶像。他们都已离世。我不知道在这里是否应该谈论在世的人，但在我看来，在我的职业领域，他们确实为教练行业的诞生奠定了基础，创造了环境。所以我会把他们也列入其中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Ken, this was such a special episode, unlike any other podcast that I've had so far. I can't wait for people to listen to it. Before I let you go, where can folks find you online if they want to reach out, learn more, and then how can listeners be helpful to you?
turns.zh: 太棒了。肯，这期播客真是特别之极，跟我迄今为止参与过的其他播客完全不同。我迫不及待想让大家收听。在你离开之前，如果听众想联系你、了解更多信息，可以在哪里找到你？又该如何为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Ken Norton
turns.en: Yeah, bringthedonuts.com is my home on the worldwide web. All my writing is there. You can get in contact with me there. I have a newsletter that I am occasionally send out, but you can find all the stuff that I've ever written and get in contact with me there. (01:13:09): The how to help be helpful question is a really easy one to answer, but that brings me a lot of joy, which is just keep being awesome product folks. You're so much my tribe. You're so close to my heart, all the work that you do, everything you bring into the world, the amazing products that we get to use that I'm sure you're working on right now that we haven't even seen yet, that you can't wait to share with us, and the cultures and teams that you make better, so your very existence. So I would say you can be helpful to me by just keep doing what you're doing.
turns.zh: 是的，bringthedonuts.com是我在网络世界的家园。我所有的作品都在那里。你可以在那里与我联系。我偶尔会发送时事通讯，但你可以在那里找到我写过的所有内容，并与我取得联系。（01:13:09）：关于如何提供帮助的问题，答案其实很简单，但这让我感到无比欣慰，那就是继续做你们出色的产品工作者。你们完全是我的同道中人。你们所做的一切工作、为世界带来的贡献、我们能使用的令人惊叹的产品（我相信你们现在正在开发尚未面世的产品，迫不及待想与我们分享），还有你们让团队和文化变得更美好的努力——你们的存在本身就是对我的帮助。所以我想说，你们可以通过继续做你们正在做的事情来帮助我。
